author: Deborah Maragopoulos, MN FNP
agent_instructions:
1. **Use the Topic Index** to find the course sections for a user's concern, and the related Q&A entries in the companion Q&A knowledge base.
2. **The Q&A knowledge base's Core Protocols (Section 0) govern dosing, timing, product use, cautions and red flags.** Where a course section differs from a Q&A canonical answer, use the Q&A answer — it is Deborah's most recent reviewed guidance. Sections with a known difference carry an **Agent caution**.
3. **Read every "Agent caution" before using a section.** Cautions mark safety points and items awaiting Deborah's confirmation.
4. **The modules were written while Deborah was in active practice.** First-person phrases like "I prescribe," "my patients" or "I check" describe her clinical experience. Deborah is not able to prescribe at this time; prescription items (thyroid medication, bioidentical hormones, dopamine agonists, estrogen, testosterone, growth hormone, metformin) are things to discuss with the user's own provider.
5. **Present outcomes as Deborah's clinical experience**, not guarantees — especially statements about what Genesis Gold or Sacred Seven do. Genesis Gold contains no hormones.
6. **The course was taught in 2017. Treat time-relative statements as of 2017, not today** ("new research published a month ago," Deborah's age in a module, "this year"). Don't present them as current.
7. **"Adrenal fatigue," "dyscircadian prolactin" and the POMC model are Deborah's clinical frameworks.** Explain them as her model of how the body works, in her words.
8. **Exercises and knowledge checks** (quoted blocks) can be offered to users as reflection prompts or journaling exercises.
9. **Red flags** (see Q&A Section 0.5, plus): postpartum confusion, hallucinations or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby → emergency care; new bulging eyes, a fast-growing neck mass, or trouble swallowing/breathing → prompt evaluation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Neuro-Immune-Endocrine System — Where East Meets West" (©D. Maragopoulos 2016): a human figure with the seven chakras on the left (Energy/East: 7th crown, 6th third eye, 5th throat, 4th heart, 3rd solar plexus, 2nd navel, 1st root) aligned with the endocrine glands on the right (West/Matter: pineal, pituitary, thyroid, thymus, adrenals, pancreas, gonads). It shows each energy center corresponding to a gland.

Welcome to Module One, Your Sex Hormones. My name is Deborah Maragopoulos FNP. I am an intuitive integrative nurse practitioner, and this document is meant to help you get your life back, starting with your sex hormones. This will include a brief foundational training for you to review, starting with the maxim: “Hormones Control Everything” When we talk about hormones, often discussed examples spring to mind, such as sex steroids, thyroid hormone, melatonin, insulin, or adrenal hormones, but I want to draw your attention to the importance of your neurotransmitters and immune system factors into your endocrine system. It may help to think of **hormones in general as the software of your human computer**. Hormones are how your body communicates with the outside world. In this document, however, we are going to focus on the sex hormones.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "DMAR® Pyramid of Health": a pyramid whose visible faces are Physiology/Biochemistry (front), Psycho-Spiritual Belief (left) and Anatomy/Structure (right), with Energy beneath it. Health depends on physiology, anatomy, environment and beliefs together.

Observe the four sides of the **DMAR Pyramid of Health** To understand your health, we must not only understand your physiology, but also your anatomy, the environment of your life, and your belief systems. All four of those pieces affect your health. Our focus will be on hormonal function. Please refer to the picture (below) depicting the physiology side of the DMAR Pyramid of Health. You will see the neuroimmune/endocrine system at the top of this facet of the pyramid, with the hypothalamus (central) controlling the facet’s entire dynamics. In later modules we will discuss how you digest, absorb, and assimilate nutrients and also the out - how you detoxify and create energy.

sections.title: The Sex Hormone Medley
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Biochemistry of the DMAR® Pyramid of Health" (©2016): the physiology face of the pyramid with the Neuro-Immune-Endocrine (NIE) system at the apex and the hypothalamus at the center orchestrating it. The base corners are IN (nutrition, digestion, assimilation) and OUT (detoxification, oxidation, energy). Caption: "Under the orchestration of the hypothalamus, hormones of the NIE sing to the DNA and the DNA dances."

But, let us return to your sex hormones, often called **steroid hormones**. And why is our focus there? Because we need to start at the base of your system. Consider this graph (below) depicting our hormonal lifespan, showing the decline of hormones over time, marked by both sexual development and middle age. It is important to understand that your body has had hormones since you were conceived. Hormones were working within you, controlling your growth in all ways throughout your life. While in fetal development, those hormones are very high. Once you reach childhood, they drop down to lower levels. In fact, if you imagine a little seven-year-old boy standing next to a little seven-year-old girl, in the nude with their genitals covered, you would find that you cannot accurately differentiate between the two, as hormones have yet to develop their bodies in adolescence. You will find that the same comparison can be made when the same pair of subjects are aged to about 90 years old. Old men start looking like women, while old women start looking like men. If you do not have active hormones, you will not develop that sex differentiation during **puberty**.

> **[Graphic]** Graph "Hormones Over the Lifespan" (©2013): hormone levels are very high in fetal life, drop to a low in childhood, surge through puberty (adrenarche, menarche/nocturnal emissions, growth hormone surges, rising BMR), peak and slowly decline through adulthood, then fluctuate and fall at midlife (adrenal, ovarian/testicular, pituitary and thyroid decline) and decline steadily through aging to death.

Puberty is the time in our lives when our hormones start to rise, and that begins with your **adrenal** hormones activating for the first time. Your sex hormones then turn on after the adrenal hormones, making the adrenals the birthplace of puberty. During puberty, some will develop breast buds and nearly all people will experience an increase in body odor, and their body hair grows. Puberty turns adolescents into that which is definitely not an adult, and yet they make an odd child.

I will never forget the very first moment that I knew that my first born was going into puberty. We were sitting on the front steps to our home. It was summertime so we both had shorts on. My child’s leg touched my leg with its new coarse adult hair and I started to cry. My little one was becoming a big adult. Children, around twelve years old, first go through menses or nocturnal emissions (or wet dreams) at this time. All people usually experience growth hormone surges and with it, growth will begin to peak. That peak usually occurs for females about 18 to 24 months after their first period, and for males this can happen anywhere from two to four years after they start their initial pubescent growth spurt. However, this can take a while and in some cases, small young men graduate from high school and will often come back from college having gained four or five inches.

Finally, the **thyroid** kicks in, which contributes to your BMR. BMR is your **basal metabolic rate** and it refers to how fast you burn energy. That is controlled by your thyroid, which only reaches full function at adulthood. Once you reach those adult levels of thyroid hormones, your system will then balance out, and you will experience the very gentle and slow decline of hormones over the years. This will continue until you reach mid -life, or the “years of the pause” - **menopause** in women and **andropause** in men. The adrenals will shut down first, then the **gonads**, ovaries and testes, will produce less sex hormones, then the pituitary will produce less growth hormone, and then the thyroid bringing up the end of this chain of aging. So as these hormones came into your life, so they will go out.

> **Exercise: P-you-berty**
> - Make a journal entry detailing your puberty
> - List which secondary sex changes you experienced, and what year and month they occured
> - It is ok to call your parents or past guardians for their memories of this time in your life

Finally, you will reach death when you no longer have the required hormones to keep your system functional. Track this temporal progression with the structure of this [this particular colorful rainbow pyramid below], the **Pyramid of Hormonal Harmony**. Therefore, to talk about sexual hormones, we must begin at the base, where you will see the gonads in that base of the pyramid.

I often have patients come to see me, believing they have a thyroid condition. At some level, they probably do, but if their sex steroids are not functioning normally, it will be difficult to get their thyroid in order. Let us say, for example, that they are not sleeping. That suggests to me that they are not producing enough melatonin, meaning that their sex hormones are not where they need to be. Without grappling with gonad problems, it will be difficult getting this patient to sleep through the night. In dealing with their pineal gland function, I must also address with their testicular or ovarian dysfunction, therefore we must likewise start at at the base of the Pyramid of Hormonal Harmony.

To illustrate why, sometimes I will have patients who want to have growth hormones so they can be younger, especially in my anti-aging group. However, I tell them, if you are not producing enough sex steroids, especially testosterone for men and estrogen for women (with a little testosterone), then we are not going to be building any rejuvenating muscle or bone. Instead, we are going to grow aspects that the patient does not need, if we give them growth hormone. So that is why we are starting at the base. But, before we continue, always remember that the **hypothalamus** is the operating system that controls everything through these hormones. Your DNA is dancing accordingly to the song of your hormones. And your Hypothalamus is the maestro of your symphony of hormones.

sections.title: The Importance of Hormonal Balance
related_qa: MEN-01 to MEN-23, PRO-01 to PRO-09
sections.text:
If you are out of tune with that hormonal song, you may be dancing like Elaine from Seinfeld, to use a dated reference, dancing eccentrically to a different drummer. Comparatively, what we want is for your body to express optimal genetic potential. Sex hormones play a role here, not only in determining your body’s shape, but also who you believe yourself to be from a gender point of view.

To explain this point further, your brain development is actually mapped out, in utero, according to the state of your sex hormones at the time. This hormonal state determines how your brain functions and who you believe yourself to be. This is definitely an issue of nature rather than an issue of nurture, as so many of the physiological contexts under which our brain operates are set during this time. We will talk further on about the effects of substances we are exposed to in utero has on our health, in so many different ways, as foreign substances can affect the the hormonal medley or the amount of hormones present in your system. The gender identity graphic below presents a rainbow coloration, hinting at the variety of sexual characteristics our body can display and the variety of gender expressions with which a person can identify. There is not a black and white dynamic here, where people are clearly male or female, certainly not when it comes to your your DNA, per se. Your genetic chromosomes may indicate XX or XY (not that all do) but how your hormones express themselves absolutely affects how your body and your brain function.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Hormones in Harmony®" (©2016): a rainbow pyramid of glands from top to bottom — pineal, pituitary, thyroid, thymus, adrenals, pancreas, gonads — with the hypothalamus as a color wheel at the center, IN and OUT at the base corners, and an arrow from the hypothalamus to a DNA strand labeled "Optimal Genetic Expression."

When your sex hormones are out of balance, women (in the graphic below) are going to notice menstrual irregularity. This will mean that their periods are coming at unpredictable times. Sometimes the woman will bleed more heavily than usual, or they will experience more cramping than most sufferers of **premenstrual syndrome**, or PMS. The sex drive tends to be lower, during a sex-hormone imbalance. You may even notice changes in your skin, such as acne or extra body/facial hair. The amount of body fat of what’s considered normal for a woman is not distributed in the same way with all people, but a woman whose hormones are out of balance will notice fat building around her middle. Such a patient may begin to lose bone mass. If her hormone levels start to drop, she may feel depressed, anxious, and she is definitely going to feel a “**brain fog**”. You may recognize that fog if you’ve ever struggled to remember why you walked into the room. You forget names, forget numbers, and forget things that you should know. It's usually short-term memory not long-term memory loss.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Your sex hormones are out of balance when…" Women: menstrual irregularity, low sex drive, acne/extra body or facial hair, thick waist, bone loss, depression/anxiety, brain fog. Men: impotency, low sex drive, belly fat, loss of muscle mass, bone loss, depression/anxiety, brain fog.

When men’s hormones are low, the effects are very similar. Some men will see issues with impotence, though they may not suffer complete impotence. Instead they experience some performance issues, such as their sex drive lowering. Men suffering sex hormone imbalance may see their motivation lowering as well, and what may increase instead, is their belly fat right around the middle. These men may be losing their muscle tone, they have signs of bone loss. Bone loss, however, usually happens a little later in men. But sex hormone imbalance also brings men feelings of depression. They may be feeling anxious and they also can suffer from that brain fog, as the same hormones are affecting their brain chemistry as with women.

> **Knowledge Check! Can you answer these questions? Check your answers against the text.**
> - Is Brain fog mostly experienced by men or women, or both?
> - What are three symptoms of hormone imbalance suffered by women?
> - True or False? PreMenstrual Syndrome is a sign of atypical hormones in women?

Now, this problem is interesting in men. I had one of my male patients, after three weeks on bioidentical testosterone replacement therapy, tell me that he did not realize how fearful he had been before. Once he was on hormone replacement, he had his confidence back. He worked in Downtown LA, not a very safe area, and he would hide his head, tuck himself in, and keep his briefcase close, hurrying between the parking lot and his office. Then testosterone replacement changed that behavior. As this example illustrates, confidence can be positively affected by balancing sexual hormones, not to mention motivation. The genders do not differ in that aspect.

sections.title: How I Understand Your Hormones — The Physical Exam
related_qa: MEN-01 to MEN-23, PRO-01 to PRO-09
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "What your body tells me…": in the physical exam Deborah reads body type, muscle mass, skin, hair, nails, reproductive organs and the general exam. Illustration of the three body types — ectomorph (lean, narrow), mesomorph (muscular), endomorph (rounder, softer) — in men and women.

So when I take a hormonally imbalanced patient’s history, I am looking for all those symptoms. However, it is when I do your physical exam that your body starts telling me what your hormones are doing. As the medium for this message, your body type will shape what your hormones say. Are you **ectomorphic**, do you tend to be slender? Are you **endomorphic**, where you tend to hold on to more body fat, or perhaps you are **mesomorphic**, and you tend to have a muscular and more athletic build. What kind of muscle mass you have contributes to the balance of your hormones. Consult the graphic above on different body types.

In fact, I can look at shirtless men on the beach, should they turn around and show me a full view, and I can tell by their shoulders and the top of their arms, where a particular muscle called the **posterior deltoid** resides, if they suffer a testosterone deficiency. Males develop that muscle on the backside (posterior) of the deltoid with the help of testosterone, which is why females have a very difficult time developing that part of the arm. In men, if that muscle flattens out, it is indicative of low testosterone or a testosterone deficiency in men. By contrast, the effects of sex hormones on women’s skin creates a more luxurious, supple, and elastic dermis than women with low estrogen. Skin supplied with ample estrogen has ample moisture in it. Of course, that means that when she loses estrogen, her skin becomes rougher and drier. Not only will we note wrinkles due to age, but also because skin loses that suppleness, that responsiveness as estrogen levels go down.

> **Body-type hype:**
> - Though society prefers us to all look like advertising models, humans have three different healthy body types.
> - Checking your hips and shoulder symmetry, which body type are you?
> - Are you Ectomorphic? Endomorphic? Mesomorphic?
> - Give your body a loving gratitude for your shape.

As another example, I had a male patient who told me that once I had put his wife on estrogen therapy he noticed a difference as her skin became more responsive to his touch. Like with male therapy, this would be **bioidentical estrogen**. So a boost in estrogen definitely affects, not only the texture of the skin, but the nerve responsiveness. Even the way the hair is distributed on a patient's body will tell me a lot about what and how much hormones they have in their system. For females, if they have **hirsutism,** which means they have hair in a male-like pattern around their chest area, especially around their nipple area. Hirsutism also causes women’s pubic hair to look more like male pattern hair.

Let us zoom in on pubic hair. Traditionally, the female pubic hair forms a triangle that points down while the male pubic hair tends to point up, ending with a little line of hair that will go towards the belly button. If I see this specific pattern on a woman’s body, that usually means she has too much DHEA and testosterone on board, and not enough estrogen. Furthermore, how healthy scalp hair looks can also demonstrate what is going on with a patient’s hormones. If I see male pattern baldness, if there is thinning on the scalp in general, not to mention the health and growth of the nails, I will conclude something is occurring with a patient’s sex hormones. And, as indicated above, what is concerning the Sex hormones must also concern the gonads, as they produce these hormones. I do a full physical exam, and if the reproductive organs feel at all outside of a normal state, then the gonads may hold the problem, such as **cysts** on the ovaries, or on the testes, which can cause hormonal imbalances.

Likewise, males with smaller testes than what I would expect for their age, may be experiencing what is called **hypogonadism**. This means that the patient does not produce enough testosterone because their testes are shrinking, just as women going through menopause - their ovaries shrink to the point where we no longer feel these gonads during a pelvic exam. When your gonads change, I detect this during a general exam, just as I detect what is going on with the heart, the lungs, the ears, the nose, and the throat. A change in your vision capabilities will also come to light in a physical exam, which may indicate that you have started to lose your hormones, so I am looking at a little bit of every factor, when I assess you.

After all, it takes a little medical detective work to discover why a patient is out of balance. What are their symptoms? When did they start puberty? What occured in their reproductive history? Did they have issues with infertility? Do they have trouble getting pregnant? Do they miscarry easily? These questions may make more sense if the patient is female. When did she go through the pause, both the perimenopause, those years before **menopause**, or **andropause** for men? If they are males experiencing an obvious testosterone deficiency, I might ask when did that start happening?

> **[Graphic]** Slide "First, medical detective work to discover why you're out of balance…": the history she takes — symptoms, puberty, reproductive history, the pause (menopause/andropause), childhood events, stress, environmental exposures, sleep, diet.

If you consulted with me, my questions might get similarly personal: What happened in your childhood that may have affected your hormones, such as major stressors, any major injuries, especially head injuries, or other diseases? Children who have gone through major treatments, I would need to know if the patient was put on steroids for asthma, or if they have undergone cancer treatments, especially radiation treatment. Too many chest x-rays or too much radiation to their **thymus ,** which is a gland in their chest, is also noteworthy. How much stress is the person being exposed to in their daily life? What are their environmental exposures, such as being exposed to heavy metals, pesticides, and toxicity? How much sleep are you getting? If you're not getting enough sleep, you're not going to be able to produce an adequate amount of hormones. Are you sleeping in the dark? Are you getting enough hours of sleep? Is it a deep enough sleep that you're dreaming? Are you remembering your dreams?

Then, what is in your diet? If you are eating a Standard American Diet (SAD), I can pretty much guarantee that your hormones are out of balance. A healthy diet will indicate more likelihood of a healthy endocrine system. All of these factors are going to affect the patient’s hormones, and determining these data points through a physical exam is a big portion of the work to getting you healthy. Clearing up your nutritional status comes next.

One of the things that patients often ask me is “How do you measure hormones?” The answer is that hormones are most accurately measured at the tissue level, but medical science barely has the capacity to perform that kind of test. Therefore, we look at the **bloodstream**, which delivers hormones to the tissues. There are no tests to look for unhealthy cells, especially to see if the **receptor sites** on those cells are functioning normally. Steroid hormones are fat-soluble: they cross the cell membrane and bind receptor sites inside the cell. If these receptor sites are blocked by toxins, the hormone cannot get into the cell. Identify the receptor site in the graphic below by the little H in a circle on the inside of the cell. Look at the cell membrane features in the image on the right, and you will see the H-shaped receptor site that steroid hormones need to get into the cell.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Steroid Hormones" (©2008): a cell membrane (phospholipid layer with glycoproteins) with a steroid receptor; the steroid hormone binds the receptor, is carried inside the cell by a chaperone protein, and acts on DNA in the nucleus. Shows how sex hormones enter cells and change gene expression.

The green chemical highlighted in the graphic is our glycoproteins and the yellow chemical is phospholipid. Let us say that your cell membrane is like a closed gate. Inside that closed gate are these little receptor sites, little openings that act like lock and key mechanisms to allow hormones entry. To interface with the cells, or to get into the cells, steroid hormones like testosterone, estrogen, progesterone, DHEA, cortisol, and aldosterone all must access the receptor site. Once they are inside, they are chaperoned by a protein all the way to the nucleus of the cell, where the hormone instructs your DNA on what to do. This is why sex hormones have often been implicated in causing cancer. But this cause for cancer is a double edged sword for cancerous growth. Because they can actually tell the DNA what to do, poetically, **progesterone** can command your DNA to stop growth, to stop cancerous growth rates in cells that should have since died. Progesterone does this by activating a cell death gene, which says “that's enough”.

sections.title: Testing sex hormones
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Chart "The menstrual cycle" (28 days; third-party graphic ©2008 Encyclopaedia Britannica): follicular phase days 0–14 with menstruation days 0–4 and a growing follicle; ovulation at day 14 triggered by an LH surge (FSH also peaks); estrogen rises before ovulation and again mid-luteal; progesterone peaks around day 21–22 in the luteal phase; the endometrial lining sheds, then thickens through the cycle.

So, we have learned that hormones change over time. They change every day, in fact. They even change throughout the month, as you can see in the menstrual cycle chart to the left. Hormones are represented by the fluctuating lines in this graphic, estrogen as a yellow line, progesterone as a blue line, **FSH** (the follicle-stimulating hormone which tells the estrogen to Surge) as a brown line, and LH in red. **LH** is a luteinizing hormone, which causes ovulation. As you can see, if I was going to measure estrogen and progesterone levels of a reproductively active woman (meaning she is still having periods), it would very much matter what day of the month it was. Your hormonal levels are not going to be the same every day of the month.

That is one reason why I don't measure estrogen or progesterone levels. I will tell you what I do measure, but first, let's compare different lab tests. If I wanted to measure your sex hormones, should that test focus on blood, urine, or saliva? What's the best measurement? Well, **urine** hormonal levels will tell me all the hormones that your body has made over the previous 24 hours, as well as those which you have detoxified and gotten rid of. So urine will give me a gist of what's in your system, but it does not really tell me hormonal activity.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Comparing lab tests": pictures of the three sample types for hormone testing — saliva collection kit, blood tubes, and urine cup.

On the other hand, I can study hormones on the tissue level through **saliva**. However, this test is momentary. Again, the day of the month, where the hormone is in its cycle, will make a big difference to this test. I'll give you an example I had of a patient doing an adrenal saliva test. This requires for spit samples first thing in the morning and again around noon, followed by one around three o'clock in the afternoon, and hopefully they wake for the final one around midnight. What we were looking for, in this case, are cortisol and DHEA levels. Things appeared straightforward and healthy at first, and then she unexpectedly tested as low in these levels. Low was to be expected, for what she was suffering, but then, at the three o'clock test, those same levels went off the charts. And so I asked her what had happened around that time. She told me that she had gone hiking and broke her ankle, a stress event which artificially elevated her cortisol. So the saliva test can be a little deceptive, you have to take it on the most representative day, which no day is. Even on such a day, it will not be indicative of your hormone levels every other day. That is why I tend to go with blood tests but I'm not exactly looking at what you would expect.

> **Self-test:**
> - Write down your hormonal medical history, specifically, which of these tests have you taken?
> - Has your Health Care Provider ever used a sub optimal test for hormones?
> - Do you still suffer the symptoms for which you made that appointment?

What I do measure, instead of straight steroid levels, is a very comprehensive blood test. I request what is called a **comprehensive metabolic panel,** which is indicative of your liver, your kidneys, and your electrolytes. I do a complete blood count, a CBC. I also check out your fasting lipid measurement, but not your typical lipid measurement. Instead, I check for lipid subparticles. I also check your CRP, your cardio reactive protein, which depicts inflammation in your cardiovascular system. I also look at your thyroid panel, which is indicated by the presence of TSH - thyroid stimulating hormone, and I check your free T4, your free T3. I look at your DHEA level, specifically the sulfated type to start with. I check your vitamin D3. I will check either a c-peptide and or hemoglobin A1c, in order to check your blood glucose issues. I also look at prolactin between 8:00 and 9:00 a.m. For women, I check FSH on day three to five of her menstrual cycle if I suspect she is perimenopausal or estrogen deficient. If she is already postmenopausal, I can check FSH at any time of the month. For men, specifically, I check their testosterone, both total and free. Sometimes I will add dihydrotestosterone to the test if they are having issues with hair loss, or if I believe they are estrogenized. If a man has too little testosterone, I will look at their sex hormone-binding globulin.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "What I check" (Deborah's standard lab panel): comprehensive metabolic panel; CBC; fasting lipid subparticles and hs-CRP; TSH, free T4, free T3; DHEA-S; vitamin D3; C-peptide/HbA1c; prolactin (8–9 a.m.); women — FSH on day 3–5 of the cycle, or anytime if postmenopausal; men — total and free testosterone, DHT, SHBG.

You do not have to remember all of this. But I wanted to demonstrate exactly the factors I am investigating. What I am looking for is not necessarily the actual numbers, but what each data point is in relationship to each other, so that I can see what is going on with the patient’s system overall.

So, why do I check cholesterol? What does that data have to do with your sex hormones? Everything, of course! Cholesterol is what your sex steroids are made from, the word steroid comes from the root “sterol”, from cholesterol. So I not only test for your total cholesterol, as well as your HDL and LDL, but I look at their particle size as well. If you imagine your cholesterol is filling up a plate - one-third of that should be HDL and two thirds should be LDL. But it gets more complex than that, because half of the HDL and half of the LDL should be large particles. The graphic below depicts the size difference in terms of small particle LDL and large particle LDL. Small particle LDL in overabundance is what causes arteriosclerosis; so if I just look at LDL, I will not be able to distinguish the balance dynamic between large and small. The typical lipid panel cannot tell the difference between the two. You might have a patient that has what looks like a normal, or even low, cholesterol level. They may even have a level of 150 mg/dL but if they have very little large LDL cholesterol to protect them and way too many small LDL cholesterol particles then the patient will have clogged arteries. Perhaps, even a heart attack, which is why particle size is so important to measure. Much more important to measure than just the totals. But if your total is rising from your baseline, if your LDL is rising from your baseline, you’re probably hormonally challenged. I treat the hormonal issue before I treat cholesterol.

> **[Graphic]** Illustration "LDL Cholesterol Balance": two LDL totals of the same value (130 mg/dL) on a scale — large, buoyant LDL particles (Pattern A) are lower risk; many small, dense LDL particles (Pattern B) are higher risk. Point: particle size (subparticle testing) matters more than the total number.

sections.title: How do Hormones control your brain?
related_qa: MEN-01 to MEN-23, PRO-01 to PRO-09
sections.text:
As I’ve previously stated, hormones control your brain. The brain on the left of the graphic below is the male brain, while the brain on the right is the female brain. The colorful lines chart the activity of your brain’s internal communication. You may notice that in the male brain, most of the communication is unilateral, meaning that communication occurs either on the right side or the left side, asymmetrically. By contrast, there is abundant crossover in the female brain. The amount of crossover is one of the key differences between the male and female brain. You may not be surprised that this difference is caused by the presence of estrogen. If a person has enough estrogen influence in the brain, as a fetus in the mother's womb, their brain will experience **crossover** by the time they are a baby of one year of age. Specifically, crossover refers to instances of the right brain talking to the left brain and vice versa. Autopsies performed on deceased babies one year of age, have found that baby boys and baby girls brains already show divergent structures due to different rates of crossover.

> **[Graphic]** Brain-connectivity illustration comparing two brains seen from above: one with connections running mostly front-to-back within each hemisphere (blue, typical male pattern) and one with dense connections crossing between the left and right hemispheres (orange, typical female pattern). Illustrates that sex hormones shape brain wiring from early life.

What I find interesting, are situations where the male baby is exposed to extra estrogen in utero, after which he will actually show crossover in the brain in non intrusive brain scans just like the image above. Estrogen absolutely influences our ability to focus on multiple things at the same time, what we call multitasking. sections.title: Sex Hormones and our Immune System
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Table "Sex hormones and immunity": in reproductive age, cell-mediated immunity is moderate (++) and antibody immunity high (++++++); postmenopausal, cell-mediated immunity is high (++++++) and antibody immunity low (++); menopausal women on HRT return to the reproductive pattern (cell-mediated ++, antibody ++++++). Shows sex hormones shift the balance between the two arms of immunity.

Sex hormones also have an effect on our immunity. The image above shows the shift in female immunity here, though sex hormones influence on immunity affects males as well. This particular study was conducted on women. We see two types of immunity, **cell mediated immunity** and **antibody immunity**. Antibody immunity is the strongest type of immunity when you are reproductively active, as that is when you are making all of your hormones, and in a female that makes sense. Antibody immunity protects against everything to which the mother’s system is being introduced. Any germs, viruses, bacteria, fungi, every foreign agent that she is being introduced to is encoded in her antibodies, which are passed on to her future offspring. So she is not in need of cell mediated immunity at this time. Cell mediated immunity can be imagined as a game of Pac-Man, where the cells act like Pac-Man, eating up foreign agents, though the antibodies do most of the work at this time.

> **Immunity Corner:**

However, when the woman becomes postmenopausal, her body switches focus from antibody immunity to cell mediated immunity. What does that change look like? The change is quite noticeable, as postmenopausal women suddenly become allergic to new substances, she may experience unexpected rashes all over her body. She may find that her body begins reacting to her soaps and her shampoos and her laundry, substances with which her antibody based immune system had no problems prior. She may even begin reacting to her own clothing. Suddenly she finds that she cannot wear polyester, it irritates her skin, which is now hyperreactive. She is reacting to foods, all because her body is transitioning to cell mediated immunity. She reports hay fever that she never experienced before, and now she struggles with sinus issues. Because her immunity has shifted, she may develop shingles — a reactivation of the chickenpox virus that has stayed dormant in her own body since childhood — because her immune system is no longer keeping that virus in check. I want to share that there is hope: If you give such a female patient hormonal replacement therapy, either conventional or bioidentical but specifically estrogen, her body will switch focus back from cell mediated immunity to antibody immunity. sections.title: Types of Sex Hormones
related_qa: MEN-01 to MEN-23, PRO-01 to PRO-09
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Table "Types of sex hormones": ESTROGEN — "the Fertilizer": estradiol; estrone, which is metabolized to "good" 2-OH estrone, "bad" 16-OH estrone and "ugly" 4-OH estrone; estriol. Estradiol range 40–400 pg/mL. PROGESTERONE — "the Gardener": converts to cortisol; range 5–20 ng/mL in the luteal phase. TESTOSTERONE — "the Motivator": converts to DHT (dihydrotestosterone) and estrogen; range 400–1600 ng/dL.

So what are the sex hormones? The three kinds are **estrogen, progesterone,** and **testosterone**. I like to refer to estrogen as “the fertilizer”. This sex hormone helps everything grow, but it does not know the difference between the body’s roses and the weeds. To solve this, all bodies also produce progesterone, though men do not produce very much of it. Progesterone is the gardener, it knows when cells have outlived their welcome and it will tell the cell “It is time for you to go now”, as previously covered in this document. Progesterone triggers the cell’s “Death Gene”, which is what happens when progesterone levels start to fall in a woman's cycle, leading to menstruation. Cells in the womb are told to die and that lining is shed.

Testosterone, our third sex hormone, is the motivator. It really is the hormone that motivates you to get things done. Testosterone is also a growth hormone. Furthermore, testosterone converts over to **dihydrotestosterone**, DHT, being the active male testosterone, and testosterone can also convert into estrogen. Males need a little estrogen, for the brain will not function without that hormone. Men do not need that much estrogen though, as too much estrogen will cause most people to feminize, including developing breast tissue. We call this specific development gynecomastia in males.

But testosterone is not the only sex hormone that is converted. Progesterone, in the middle column, converts to **cortisol**, which is an adrenal hormone. It is one of the adrenal stress hormones that heightens when a woman is under a lot of stress. Let's take a bride, for example. She is getting ready to be married and comes to me, her health care provider, wanting to regulate her menstrual cycle before her wedding so she doesn't get her period on her honeymoon. We do our darndest to accomplish that. In this case we would use bioidenticals. You can even use birth control for this purpose, in its common pill form. But, almost invariably, that stressed out bride will have her period on her wedding day or honeymoon. This happens because most of the progesterone that we are giving her, as well as the progesterone she naturally produces, is being converted to the stress hormone cortisol. Cortisol does not keeping her lining stable.

Estrogen, on the other hand, is converted to three smaller types of estrogen; the active estrogen, known as **estradiol**, is converted into **estrone**, while this long acting estrogen gets converted into **estriol**. All these conversion processes happens via the liver and in the fat cells. Now, there are three types of estrone, I call them the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly. **2- hydroxyl estrone** is the good one. The bad estrone is **16- hydroxyl**, bad meaning that it causes inflammation. But the really ugly conversion creates **4-hydroxyl estrone**, which triggers cancers. Premarin is found in abundance in pregnant mare’s urine, which is one of the first estrogens we have used in medicine for hormone replacement therapy. The only thing Premarin can be converted into in the human body is 4-hydroxyl estrone. Now, why is it not that every woman who takes Premarin gets cancer, especially breast cancer? That is because cancer is a multifactorial disease, not only caused by the estrogen.

> **Exercise: Draw it out!**
> - Draw out the conversion process between your sex hormones
> - Don’t forget to add the products of your sex hormones!

Estriol is your pregnancy hormone. Your body makes a lot of it when you are pregnant. You make less of it when you are not pregnant. It is the safest of these hormones, but it can be converted back into 16-hydroxyl estrone. Refer back to the image at the top of this section, notice the bottom row, the amounts of estrogen, compare the difference in prevalence in each sex hormone. Estradiol in the body can be found at a measure of 40 to 400 picograms per milliliter. That number, unique to each patient, is changing every day. Now look at the figures for male hormones. Testosterone is measured at 400 to 1600 nanograms per deciliter. Now look at progesterone, at 5 to 20 nanograms per milliliter. Remember that the units differ: 1 deciliter equals 100 milliliters.

So if your body is actually making much more progesterone than estrogen and testosterone, if I maintained the same units of measurement, then progesterone would not show up on the chart, that’s how much more of it is in our systems.

sections.text:

It is why males tend to wake up at this time, if they have healthy testosterone levels, then they will wake up with a morning erection. Men who work graveyard shifts, such as my husband who was a police officer for many years, actually have that five AM surge while they are young but as they get older they may no longer see the surge due to missing sleep from graveyard shifts. **BPA**, finally we have BPA. BPA is found in plastics. BPA is bisphenol A, a type of plastic that we have been creating since the 1950s. Bisphenol A is a kind of plastic that acts as an endocrine disruptor, meaning that the chemical, BPA, interferes with your hormone’s entry into your cells. BPA tends to have an estrogenic effect. In the early days of this treatment, when we first prescribed birth control pills, the doses were enough to stop an elephant from reproducing. We no longer prescribe that high level of dosage, and I am not a believer in women over the age of 35, or 30 if they're a smoker, taking oral hormones. We do not administer testosterone orally. The dose is either injectable or able to be rubbed on the skin. As you can see, there are different places on the body that will accept hormones, and they each do so differently. Of great importance is the medium of delivery. The hormonal cream base needs to be liposomal or fat based. If it is an alcohol base, the cream will not absorb into the body as well. Let us talk about your gut. Our healing actually occurs from the inside out. It may help to imagine yourself like a human donut. Your skin protects you from the outside world and your gut protects you from the inside world. While the skin does absorb some water and creates vitamin D, our skin does not have as much function as our gut does. The gut has what is called the transpermeable membrane which allows you to absorb your nutrients, but keeps toxins out. This feature is incredibly important for your body to have everything it needs to build a new you, as well as keep the outside world at bay.

> **[Graphic]** Illustration of the digestive organs (stomach, small intestine, colon) drawn over a woman's abdomen.

The problem that most of us experience is that our guts are not as healthy as they could be. When you do have optimal gastrointestinal function, your hormones are more balanced. This is because your gut affects your pituitary gland, your hypothalamus, your pancreas, your ovaries or testes, as well as affecting your thyroid, and your adrenal glands. Thereby affecting not only the function of these glands through nutrition, but how those hormones are metabolized. Basically how they are removed from your system, whether through detoxification or by being recycled back into the system again. Many of my **estrogen dominance** women patients, experiencing too much estrogen on board, are not suffering from a production issue. Instead, estrogen dominance is often a recycling issue, due to the gut being out of balance, these patients are recycling an excess of estrogen. In these cases, the liver may be trying to arrest this circular system while the bacteria in the gut are removing the chemical handcuffs on that estrogen and allowing that estrogen to be recycled back into the bloodstream again to work as before. Therefore it is incredibly important that the gut stays healthy for your hormonal balance.

Your gut is also connected to your brain. As discussed in the first of these modules, the hypothalamus controls your immune system, your hormones, and your brain function. But your brain is not the only brain you have, you also have a brain in your heart, and a brain in your gut. All three of those “brains” produce the same neurotransmitters. We now know that your gut has a deep relationship with your brain. For instance, the bacteria in your gut, whether good, bad, or indifferent, will talk to your brain and tell it what to do. It will actually tell your hypothalamus what to do.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Optimal GI function = balanced hormones": the intestines at the center with arrows to the adrenal glands, hypothalamus and pituitary, pancreas, thyroid, and ovary/testis — gut health feeds every hormone-producing gland.

Studies involving fecal implants (where a researcher takes the feces of a healthy person, encapsulates it, and administers it to someone who is really sick- such as with C difficile) have shown successful implantation of healthy bacteria into the subjects. We will discuss this technique more later. We have learned that, if the healthy bacteria comes from a donor who is overweight and was put into a subject who has normal weight, the normal weight subject will become obese. The bacteria donated by the obese person communicates to the subject’s hypothalamus, informing it on how much food the gut needs, which causes the thin person to become obese. From this example, we see that it is incredibly important that we keep our gut healthy, because the gut and the brain communicate.

Your gut also affects your immunity, being one of your first lines of defense. If your immune cells are healthy in the gut and your bacteria community is healthy in your gut, this is a sign that your immune system is working properly. If the bacterial community, sometimes called your **bacterial flora**, is out of balance then you may have what is called bacterial dysbiosis**. Bacterial Dysbiosis** occurs when our bacteria, both our helpful bacteria and our harmful bacteria are out of balance with one another, causing us to develop immune disorders. Most immune disorders are related to autoimmunity and allergies; as are metabolic disorders, like metabolic syndrome, in which one suffers from high blood glucose, hypertension, heart disease.

The following is a little tour of our gut. Let us start with the mouth, the beginning of your gastrointestinal tract. In your mouth, you start digestion via saliva and mastication, or chewing of your food. In fact, just thinking about food will start saliva production and a hormonal reaction that tells the stomach to tell the small intestine to tell the liver and the gallbladder that food is coming. That food, once swallowed, goes down the esophagus and enters into the stomach via a sphincter opening. Just like the anal sphincter, this opening is a tight little round muscle that allows food to go into the stomach and keeps the food from coming back up. When you suffer heartburn, indigestion, or when you are vomiting, that sphincter is not working properly; it is allowing the food to come back up into the esophagus when food is supposed to stay down.

sections.text:
In the stomach, the food is introduced to an incredibly acidic environment. The hydrochloric acid of the stomach is rated at a pH of 1. To put this in perspective, water has a pH of 7, which is neutral. PH 1 is very acidic, but it needs to be in order for you to be able to digest proteins and fats. You have to break down your food in the stomach, the first level of digestion. If you do not produce enough hydrochloric acid, you suffer from a condition called **hypochlorhydria**. Your body needs this acidic organ. If the stomach does not make enough acid, malnourishment follows. Conversely, a stomach making too much acid is almost never an issue. The issue with an acidic stomach, called **gastritis** or heartburn, is that the stomach itself does not have enough mucus. There are **mucin cells** in the stomach that line the organ and allow it to produce enough mucus to protect itself from its own acids.

If you have ever been to the ocean, playing around the tide pools, and you saw sea anemones, with their little mucus-covered sticky fingers, then you have seen how the inside of a stomach functions. These external “Fingers” are actually their stomach which catches fish, produces digestive acid, and that mucus layer makes sure the acid does not digest the sea anemone. The acid that digests your food is not supposed to start breaking down your stomach lining, therefore; if you are not producing enough mucus in your stomach you will end up having gastritis which can cause that stomach sphincter to become irritated. You will start eructating, or belching, as the food and acid comes up into the esophagus. We call that burning in your esophagus, in your chest, heartburn. This acid and food solution can travel all the way up into your mouth and eat away the enamel of your teeth. Sometimes severely sore throats are not caused by the common cold, but from acid in the throat. As you can see, keeping that stomach acid in balance and keeping the stomach in balance is really important. There is a type of bacteria, called H pylori, that lives in your stomach that can become overgrown, causing gastritis. This bacteria is transmitted from your primary caretaker, often your mother. It is usually passed through saliva, through kissing and sharing food as a child, but it can become an issue when you get older.

> **Exercise: Harping on Heartburn**
> - If you suffer heartburn, make note in a calendar of when you experience it
> - Note patterns in your calendar, what you eat or do that could contribute to the problem
> - Work on addressing these causes

sections.module_title: Your Gastrointestinal Tract and Hormonal Balance
sections.title: The Small Intestines, Gallbladder, and Liver
sections.text:
So let us follow the food through your digestive tract a little further. Once it leaves the stomach, food goes through another sphincter at the bottom of the stomach and enters the small intestine, the job of which is to perform the major digestion. Aiding this organ is the pancreas, by producing digestive enzymes, but not before the gallbladder dumps a sizable amount of bile into the mix. Why is bile so necessary for the small intestine’s process? Because bile is so incredibly alkaline that it actually neutralizes the stomach acid that is delivered through the lower stomach sphincter with the food, so that food from the stomach with a pH of 1 immediately becomes neutralized by the bile, with its pH of 9. The result will be a ph of around 7 in the small intestine, though it ranges between 6.8 and 7.2. The small intestine’s environment needs to be neutral so the pancreatic enzymes can function. If those pancreatic enzymes are working properly, then digestion will occur. Digestion, in this case, means the breakdown of the food in the small intestine.

Let us discuss the Gallbladder in more detail. The job of the gallbladder is to store the **bile acids** produced by the liver. Those bile acids is what starts breaking down your fat from big molecules into smaller molecules, which then allows the fat to be processed by the digestive enzymes that breakdown fat, called **lipases**. Proteases break down proteins and there is lots of other “-ases” to break down sugar, like amylase and lactase etc. While the food is in your small intestine these enzymes assist in breakdown of the food, both micronutrients and macronutrients. **Micronutrients** are the vitamins, minerals and coenzymes; while **macronutrients** are carbohydrates, proteins and fats, which get absorbed through the small intestines’ membranes and into the blood vessels coating the entire small intestine. These nutrients are absorbed through the villi into the blood vessels of the **mesentery**, which conduct both macronutrients and micronutrients directly into the large blood vessels that go to the liver. The liver is the next stop, for our food, where it gets filtered for toxins before it is released into the body.

sections.module_title: Your Gastrointestinal Tract and Hormonal Balance
sections.title: The Large Intestine or Colon
sections.text:
So whatever material is left over from the previous digestive process passes from the small intestine through the **ileocecal valve**, the gateway to the large intestine. If your pyloric sphincter and your ileocecal valve are out of sync with one another, a synchronicity arranged via hormones in the gut, then you will end up dumping your undigested food too quickly, causing diarrhea. Furthermore, if the ileocecal valve stays open, sometimes the bacteria from the colon travels into the small intestine and that will cause the condition called **small intestinal bacterial overgrowth**, which causes all kinds of problems with digestion as well.

So now this digested material, the leftovers as well as any toxins that had to come out of the liver, end up in the **large intestine**, also called the **colon**, where the colon’s job is to form stools out of it.. The colon sucks the water out of the material, but not the toxins. This organ is aided by its own culture of bacteria that work to ferment all of this material, eating the fiber and whatever nutrients are left over. That is why it is so important that you include ample fiber in your diet. You must keep these friendly bacteria alive, so that they can help you. This bacteria culture actually helps to activate some of your vitamins, the last of the vitamins, so they might be absorbed through the colon walls. These bacteria, including lactobacillus acidophilus, bifidobacterium, and E coli are actually protecting you from pathogens while activating these remaining vitamins for last minute digestive absorption.

As the stool passes through this long intestine (about 5 feet long versus the small intestine, which is about 20 feet though much smaller in diameter compared to the large intestine) the organ is slowly pulling out the water from the material, forming the stool. If the colon pulls out too much water, you will be constipated. If the colon pulls out too little water then you experience diarrhea. Eventually the stool ends up in the **rectal vault** and you defecate through the anus. The **intestinal villi,** seen to the right using an electron microscope, line the walls of your small intestine. Note the little **enterocytes**, the cells of the intestine that allow the nutrition in but keep the toxins out. You can see the rich layer underneath, where the bloodstream or capillary bed is that allows those nutrients to get into the rest of the body.

> **[Graphic]** Microscope image of intestinal villi — the finger-like projections of the small-intestine lining that absorb nutrients.

sections.text:
Now we will break what we have just learned into distinct pieces and explain why each are integral to understanding **Gastrointestinal Dysfunction**. What are some of the symptoms of GI dysfunction? One of the biggest symptoms is **indigestion** or **heartburn**, but also **bloating** after you eat. If your stomach feels bloated or if you feel uncomfortable with gas, such as with **belching** and **flatulence**, those are signs that things could be out of balance. You may be internally fermenting your food, almost like you are brewing beer or raising bread in your belly. **Diarrhea** and **constipation** are also signs of gastrointestinal dysfunction. Unusual **sensitivities to specific foods** is also a sign of gastrointestinal dysfunction, and does not necessarily mean you have an allergy. These symptoms indicate that you are out of balance in your gut

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Symptoms of GI dysfunction": indigestion and heartburn; bloating after meals; gas (belching and flatulence); diarrhea; constipation; food sensitivities; acne, eczema, rashes; allergies and asthma; mood disorders; learning disabilities; weight issues; autoimmunity; thyroid and adrenal issues; sex hormone imbalance.

Issues with your skin, such as **acne**, **eczema**, and certain **rashes**, are also signs of gastrointestinal imbalance. To briefly explain why that is, there are three ways out of our body for toxins to exit. One is through your colon, the second is via your kidneys, and the third way is through your skin. If ingested toxins are being introduced into the bloodstream they are going to have to get out, if the kidneys cannot handle it then your skin is the way out. This can cause skin allergies, acne and eczema, all signs of immune system disorders related to the gut.

Mood disorders like **depression** and **anxiety** can also be caused by gut dysfunction. Learning disabilities like **autism**, **attention deficit disorder**, can be related to gut dysfunction as well. Weight issues of course, either being **underweight** or **overweight**, are often a sign of an imbalance in the GI flora (see **Bacterial flora** in the introduction). If not a bacterial imbalance, these issues may be caused by an imbalance in your guts’ ability to properly digest foods and absorb nutrients. Moreover, **autoimmunity**, **lupus**, **rheumatoid arthritis**, **thyroiditis**, **Hashimoto’s thyroiditi**s, all of the distinct **Sjogren’s disease**, **psoriasis**, each of these autoimmune diseases have been related to gastrointestinal dysfunction, imbalances in the gut, and a dysfunction in the colon lining.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Your gut health affects your…": the intestines with arrows to the brain, skin, muscles and skeleton (body/movement), adrenal glands, thyroid, and ovary/testis.

Not only can such disorders be traced to GI dysfunction, but many **hormonal disorders** can also cause GI dysfunction. **Thyroid disorder**s and **adrenal** issues affect the gut’s function, and are in turn affected by the gut’s function. It is no different with sex hormones, which are also affected by the gut’s function and can contribute to GI dysfunction. As previously mentioned, estrogen recycling is dependant on a balanced GI tract, without such balance Estrogen may collect in excess or dominance in the body when it should be extracted by your gut and defecated out. So your gut health affects your adrenal glands, your thyroid, your ovaries and testes, your musculoskeletal system, joints, skin, and your brain. As you can see, there is not much of you that your gut does not affect.

sections.title: Testing for Gastrointestinal Dysfunction
sections.text:
How do we assess GI dysfunction? There are a couple of home tests that can be performed while other tests require laboratory work to investigate your gut. The first home test is the **Apple Cider Vinegar Test**. This test will determine if you are making enough hydrochloric acid in your stomach. We recommend using organic and filtered apple cider vinegar for this test, and you can perform it yourself by drinking about a teaspoon to a tablespoon of apple cider vinegar before you go to bed. If you wake up in the morning with a noticeably reduced acid stomach, experiencing less gastritis, less heartburn, than you normally do, this proves that you are hypochlorhydria - meaning you don’t make enough gastric acid. So, if you are having problems with indigestion, you can test your hydrochloric acid production by taking a dose of apple cider vinegar right before bed.

Now the **Beet Test** will be familiar to my patients and students. Beets have a certain dye in it that is very pink and is not completely removed over the course of the normal length of digestion. To preserve the dye, do not use beets that have been pickled; do roast or saute them instead. Even raw beets will work. What will happen within 12 to 24 hours after eating the beets is that the pink should be visible in your stool if your digestion is occurring in a healthy period of time. If you see the pink dye in your stool too soon after ingestion, less than 12 hours then you are suffering a rapid transit time, meaning your nutrition is being processed too quickly for extraction. A likely byproduct of this disorder is diarrhea. However, if it takes longer than 24 hours to see the pink in your stool, then you have a delayed transit time, from which you are more likely to have constipation. Both are indications of a GI imbalance.

*[Image: a bottle of raw, unfiltered apple cider vinegar "with the mother" and a fresh beet with greens (foods used to support stomach acid and bile/digestion).]*

As for laboratory tests, the FIRST is called a **Functional Stool Test**, complete with Digestive Stool Analysis with parasitology. This indicates that the laboratory will be taking an inventory of all the bacteria that is growing within your GI, as well as all the digestive enzymes present in your stool. This test allows us to qualify your gut’s functioning by looking at your byproduct. After being collected, the stool sample is sent to a lab, where the testing is completed. We will look at the results of such a test in greater detail, but first another laboratory test bears mentioning. This is a test of the subject’s breath which looks for H pylori. H. pylori is the previously mentioned stomach bacterium that can cause gastritis and potentially gastric cancer.

sections.title: Understanding Digestive Stool Analysis
sections.text:
Let us take a closer look at a CDSA, a Comprehensive Digestive Stool Analysis. We will provide an overview of the stool analysis and detail what lab technicians and Health Care Providers look for in the results. Please reference the image below.

> **[Graphic]** Sample stool-test report (Genova "GI Effects Comprehensive Profile — Interpretation At-a-Glance"). It groups results into four categories: Infection; Inflammation (calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin, EPX, fecal secretory IgA); Insufficiency (total fecal fats — poor fat digestion); Imbalance (potentially pathogenic bacteria, beneficial bacteria, n-butyrate, beta-glucuronidase). It also shows a diversity scale (higher vs lower microbial diversity) and a bar chart comparing the patient's relative abundance of bacterial phyla (Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, etc.) with a healthy group. Arrows mark which markers are high or low.

sections.title: Reading the Stool Test: Infection, Inflammation, Insufficiency, Imbalance
sections.text:
First we begin with any sign of infection and, in this sample, there is an obvious lack of data, so this subject did not have an infection. However, they have many markers for:

- **Inflammation**.These markers can include

- Calprotectin- which is actually a marker that indicates inflammation related to colitis and immune disorders

- Fecal Lactoferrin- another marker of inflammation, indicates intestinal inflammation

- EPX- this is basically a marker that is related to allergies, particularly to foods and food sensitivities

- Fecal Secretory IgA- is your first line of defense and if this is out of balance it also indicates you have an imbalance in your immune system.

- **Insufficiency**. If you are not digesting your foods properly, you will have some form of enzymatic insufficiency, which means that you are not making enough pancreatic enzymes. Here we see an increase, in this case, of:

- Fecal Fats- however this could also indicate the presence of improperly broken down proteins

- **Imbalance** If you have an imbalance in your gut bacteria, that is going to show in this section. This subject shows evidence of:

- Pathogenic Gut Bacteria

- Beneficial bacteria, if you have enough of them, which this subject does not

- Butyrate Imbalance- Butyrate is made by beneficial bacteria from fiber and feeds the cells of your colon; if you do not make enough of it, then you are probably not eating enough fiber to feed your beneficial bacteria

> **[Graphic]** (Same stool-test report graphic as above.)

- Beta glucuronidase is an enzyme that unlocks the bonds placed on hormones that have been chemically handcuffed. These handcuffs prevent the hormones from being reabsorbed by your gut, so they can be defecated out. If you make too much Beta glucuronidase, these hormones will be released back into your body, causing an imbalance of hormone recycling, such as estrogen dominance. You may also experience high levels of testosterone, or high adrenal hormones, all because this unlocking enzyme is over produced.

- **Diversity**- which refers to diversity of bacteria. Not only lactobacillus acidophilus, bifidus and E.coli previously mentioned, but a whole ecosystem of bacteria. The more variety of the millions of bacteria species we host in our gut the healthier your gut is.

- In this case this subject has low variety. If you look at the abundance the healthy cohort of diversity looks like this. This subject looks mostly healthy, but has too much of some bacteria, and is missing others. See the next section.

- **Relative Abundance** indicates the type of bacteria in question. Listed are the phylums, or the families of bacteria that we would normally see in the healthy human gut.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "What your tests tell me…": maldigestion/malabsorption, intestinal dysbiosis, irritable bowel syndrome, leaky gut syndrome. Inset "Good and bad bacterial flora": beneficial bifidobacteria, E. coli strains and lactobacilli versus harmful Campylobacter, Enterococcus faecalis and Clostridium difficile.

This colorful test is rich in information, but requires an expert to interpret. What does this kind of test tell this particular practitioner? Well, it will tell me if you have maldigestion or malabsorption. To say that another way, are you digesting your foods properly and are you absorbing them properly? Do you have intestinal dysbiosis? Do you have enough of any strain of good bacteria, such as bifidus bacteria, E coli, or lactobacillus or perhaps you are missing some? Do you have some of these bad bacteria, including campylobacter, enterococcus, clostridium difficile? That last strain is responsible for a severe diarrhea disease. In fact, irritable bowel syndrome is one of the conditions that we can see in these results. Notice how some of those inflammatory markers will be elevated in irritable bowel syndrome and colitis. We can also see symptoms of this in leaky gut syndrome, depending on the markers in the rest results. So, the complete digestive stool analysis is a truly effective tool to check in on what is happening in your gut, it is a mainstay in gut health.

sections.title: A Healthy Gut and a Leaky Gut
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Healthy gut vs. leaky gut": in a healthy gut, intestinal cells are sealed by tight junctions so only nutrients reach the bloodstream. Antibiotics, autoimmunity, unhealthy diet, dysbiosis, infections, low stomach acid, NSAIDs, stress and toxins lead to leaky gut — compromised junctions let pathogens and undigested food particles into the bloodstream, triggering immune cells, antibodies and food sensitivities, and reducing nutrient absorption.

So what does a healthy gut look like? The above left side is an illustrated picture that depicts the cross section of a healthy gut . Notice the exceptionally tight junctions, meaning that each one of these **enterocytes** are close to their neighbors. Now, on the right you will see an unhealthy gut, also known as a **leaky gut**, where we can see the junctions have been broken. Above this colon landscape, what you see moving across are bacterium. On the right side, these cultures are getting through the loose junctions. We have toxins, food sensitivities, and all kinds of matter getting through to the bloodstream.

The healthy gut, by contrast, is nice and tight. We have got healthy bacteria. In the healthy gut we have healthy looking cells; while the cells of the leaky gut wall of the organ have seperated into the gaps you see, almost like Swiss cheese. This is due to the **anterior** sites of the enterocytes cells being far apart and allowing unabsorbed food particles to get into your system, which creates antibody reactions in your bloodstreams. Normally you would be defecating this food, as you are done with it. As you don’t need it anymore, if it gets into your bloodstream through your leaky gut, antibodies will respond.

Leaky guts have a variety of possible causes. You can contract a leaky gut from taking unhealthy amounts of **antibiotics**, which kills off all of your good bacteria. It is also possible to gain a leaky gut if you have an autoimmune disorder and your immune system is not functioning properly. Of course, if your diet is unhealthy, depriving you of enough variety of bacteria cultures, that can also cause a Leaky Gut. A poor diet may mean possibly lacking fermented foods or yogurt, in which those beneficial cultures can be found, causing an imbalance in your gut bacteria. **Infections**, too, will cause increased risk of leaky gut, as can low amounts of stomach acid, as we discussed previously.

If you suffer any of these conditions then you are more likely to get leaky guts. Which means that you are not going to digest your foods properly, leaving yourself with undigested food that is irritating to the gut lining and causing inflammation. Even non-antibiotic medication can contribute to this problem such as with **NSAIDS**. These include aspirin and ibuprofen, naproxen, and Aleve. When these drugs are taken for longer periods of time than necessary it will actually cause irritation in the gut. This results in decreased prostaglandins, and depriving your stomach and small intestine of the ability to protect themselves from digestive enzymes and stomach acids.

The mind is also an offender. Stress raises your cortisol levels, and those copious amounts of cortisol start eating away at the colon lining. **Cortisol** is one of those hormones that is **catabolic**, meaning it breaks down tissues (conversely, **anabolic** means building up). Cortisol is made by the body to act catabolic against inflammation but it is not supposed to break down healthy cells! Therefore, if you have too much stress and your cortisol levels are high, your body will eat away your own tissues - including the lining of your small intestine and create this leaky gut. Do be sure to look out for toxins, as some toxins are so irritating to the gut lining, they act as a catabolic. Pesticides, metals, and many food additives all count as toxins in this way, causing issues with inflammation, irritation and eventually a leaky gut.

sections.title: Treating Gastrointestinal Dysfunction
sections.text: Once we understand your dis-ease, we can work on getting you back to ease. So how do we treat gut dysfunction.? In my methods, there are three R’s, we need to remove, repair and replace. We need to remove what is hurting the gut, we need to repair the lining of the gut, and we need to replace with good bacterium in the gut lining. Let us begin.

sections.module_title: Your Gastrointestinal Tract and Hormonal Balance
sections.title: Step 1. Remove
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "REMOVE" (step 1 of gut healing): offending foods — alcohol, garlic and onions, red meat, whole grains, dairy, citrus, butter, chocolate, deep-fried foods (common triggers to remove based on testing) — and pathogens (bacteria, fungi/yeast, parasitic worms).

The first item for removal are any offending foods. Identifying these foods can be a simple matter, as the patient may be seeking medical attention around these reactions. It also helps that many food susceptible to sensitivity are known and recorded, and most people have reactions to certain foods that they know about. However, in the case of a reaction to an unknown food, we are not without tests to determine the culprit. There is a method called **IgG testing**, which allows us to see which food groups to which the dis-eased might be reacting to. It is important to distinguish these sensitivities from allergies.

For instance, If we know you routinely experience flatulence and bloating when you eat garlic and onions, then we are going to remove those foods from your diet. It would be the same for any particular citrus, alcohol, or red meat that irritates you, we must remove these foods from your system while you recover. There is no need to say goodbye to these foods for good, as we may reintroduce some of these foods later. However, in the immediate we will get the irritation out of the system, so we must take away the offending foods.

Reintroduction may take six to eight weeks after we have healed your GI tract to reintroduce the foods again, with an eye toward your health. This means unhealthier foods, such as french fries, may never be healthy for you to reintroduce to your system. We must also remove any **pathogens** if we find any in your gut. Pathogens can include bacterium, fungus, yeast, candida, and parasites, such as worms. We must remove these pathogens because if we do not, they are going to continue irritating your gut, preventing us from healing that gut lining.

sections.module_title: Your Gastrointestinal Tract and Hormonal Balance
sections.title: Step 2. Repair
sections.text:
After removing irritants and pathogens, we are ready to repair the gut. There are multiple different methods to go about this. First there is **L-glutamine**, an amino acid of glutamine that can be found in meat, a tried and trusted method for gut repair. The enterocytes react very well to L-glutamine, in fact they require a steady intake of it. If you don’t eat an adequate amount of protein, breaking it down yourself, you are not extracting enough glutamine to repair your gut, specifically, your gastrointestinal lining.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "REPAIR" (step 2): turmeric, chamomile, mint and L-glutamine powder — substances that soothe and rebuild the gut lining.

A less carnivorous approach would be to use Chamomile, which is soothing in the gut. Mint, as well, has a soothing effect on the colon, as does the spice turmeric. In fact, there are many different herbs and nutritional supplements that can heal your large intestine, but I recommend using a healing agent particular to your needs, as determined by your gut analysis, not just any medicine. I introduced L-glutamine, chamomile, mint, and turmeric because these are substances that can be safely used for most colons. When working with patients, I use the complete digestive stool analysis to determine specific causes and effects of your irritation and inflammation. The medicine I chose for your body will be specific for your case. Depending on what the lab tests call for, I may include antibiotics to kill bacteria or I may use an antimicrobial herb. A patient’s particular sensitivities, as determined by testing will be my guide.

sections.module_title: Your Gastrointestinal Tract and Hormonal Balance
sections.title: Step 3. Replace
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "REPLACE" (step 3): beneficial gut bacteria (probiotics) in the colon and a jar of fermented vegetables.

Third, we will need to replace with good bacterium. This may include lactobacillus acidophilus or bifidus bacterium; however, you cannot replace E.coli without a **fecal transplant**. Though that is the difficult case, it is possible. As described above, a fecal transplant uses stool from a screened human donor. This may disgust, but in the animal kingdom separate species will ingest each other’s feces to replace with good bacteria. People are less motivated to try this, and I do not recommend oral ingestion in any case. What follows is a less controversial method, that still challenges our sensibilities. Our first world mentality causes us to eschew dirt and because of this we are clean beyond what is healthy. We are not accustomed to eating dirt, choosing to clean it off of us at every opportunity. However, one of the best methods to get microbial variety in your gut is to go out and **get your hands dirty in the soil**, soil that has not been treated with pesticides or toxins. Additionally, do not be so fastidious about cleaning your hands before meals. You need that dirt. Studies have show than children who are exposed to dirt when they were young have healthier immune systems and healthy guts.

sections.title: Going Further: Fermentation
sections.text:
If those methods do not appeal to you, I have another alternative to eating dirt: try fermented foods. To speak plainly, **fermentation** is the process of putting foods [like in this case the bunch of different vegetables] in a container, packed with salt. We allow the food to actually start to **macerate**, or soften with the salt, so that the foods start releasing their fluids and juices. This allows the bacteria and microorganisms, naturally living on the skins of these vegetables, fruits, or herbs, to start the fermentation process. The food in the container will have revitalized as live organisms, and those live organisms need to be eaten. Most cultures have some form of fermentation in their diet, whereas our culture tends to pasteurize everything to sterilize the live cultures out of our diet. One of the best and easiest ways to get fermented food is in **greek yogurt**, but you could do with East Asian **kombucha tea**, or Korean **kimchi.** There are many different types of fermented foods available, benefiting from centuries of practice to provide a variety of bacteria to your gut’s microscopic diversity.

> **Exercise: Fermentation Diet**
> - Make a list of the kinds of fermented food you’ve eaten before
> - Circle the foods you like or are readily available in your community
> - Plan to eat these foods on a weekly basis
> - Write in your calendar when you eat a favorite/available food from your list
> - Begin noting your indigestion and GI issues in your calendar or journal
> - Cross reference your fermented food intake with how you feel

sections.text:
