sections.text:
This document is focused on inflammation and immunity, which I find is an opportunity to underline the trigger of many diseases - lack of sleep. If I could recommend that you do one thing for your health, one practice that will make the biggest difference to your health, is getting an adequate amount of sleep. This is necessary for your body and for aging gracefully, because lack of sleep affects so many aspects of health.

> **[Graphic]** Infographic of the effects of sleep deprivation on the body: accidental death, yawning, memory problems, hallucinations, micro-sleeps, weakened immune response, weight gain, high blood pressure, impaired brain activity, cognitive dysfunction, moodiness, depression, being accident-prone, colds and flu, type 2 diabetes, heart disease.

So, what you can see in the image above, is how broadly a **lack of of sleep** actually affects your body. Insufficient sleep increases your vulnerability to disease and weakens your immune system. What is more, you are increasingly likely to get colds and flu, develop insulin resistance, gain weight, and develop type 2 diabetes. Without proper sleep, you are more likely to gain high blood pressure, develop heart disease, and worsen moodiness. Those who go without sleep can suffer or worsen depression, anxiety, and even hallucinations. Getting enough sleep maximizes your memory, cognitive function, ability to think, focus, and concentrate. Comparatively, **brain activity** is impaired with less sleep. As a medical practitioner, I have observed increase in accidental deaths associated with poor sleep, probably due to a decrease in ability to coordinate actions and make clear judgments. You may know from experience that you do not feel well when you do not get enough sleep, that feeling corresponds to measurable effects at the biochemical level. Read on to find out why this lack of sleep is so widespread.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "What happened to our sleep?" — Gallup survey of usual hours of sleep: in 1942, 84% slept 7+ hours (average 7.9 hours; only 11% slept 6 hours or less); by 1990–2013 only 56–59% slept 7+ hours, about 40% slept 6 hours or less, and the average fell to 6.7–6.8 hours.

So, what happened to our sleep, as a society. Let me tell you about an interesting study from the Gallup Polling service, seen on the image above, that compared the hours of sleep people reported in data taken in 1942 compared to a similar survey from 1990, then from 2013. As you can see, the average hours of sleep per night was almost eight hours in 1942, but decreased to under seven hours average in 2013. What change actually occurred? I believe that the factor with the highest likelihood of affecting this change is the greater adoption of electric power, with people staying up later under yellow light bulbs, also with television programming being aired after dark. However, the shifts in less sleep around 1990 and again in 2000 were most likely caused by computer screens. Work and entertainment both engendered screen viewing later and later at night. **These lights really affect your ability to sleep**.

sections.title: Causes of Sleep Loss — Eating Habits
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "Sleep thieves": screens, late heavy meals (burger and fries), artificial light, stress/overwork, and alcohol.

Science has documented that when we eat too heavily, you are going to actually not sleep as well. Many people in this condition will experience hot flashes and become uncomfortable. They may even wake up in the middle of the night, especially older people, believing they are having menopausal hot flashes when they are actually suffering a liver issue from having eaten too heavily. **Eating too close to bedtime,** especially a high fat meal, forces your liver to overwork in the middle of the night. This raises your body temperature higher, causing the apparent hot flashes. Eating later pushes your comfortable time frame of finding sleep later as well.

sections.title: Causes of Sleep Loss — Light
sections.text: Light is an essential factor in our sleep. Keeping any lights on in your room will steal a person’s healthy sleep. Now, some people are incredibly light sensitive. I know that I am very light sensitive, even when staying in a hotel room I must cover all the various digital lights throughout the room. Now, people may find that they become less light sensitive the more light they are exposed to, though they seem to be sleeping - these people miss out on deep REM sleep. If you expose yourself to these **blue screens**; computer screens, television screens, little tablets, and touchscreen phones, you will suffer a suppression of melatonin production and decrease the depth of your sleep.

sections.title: Causes of Sleep Loss — Stress and Alcohol
sections.text: It is incontrovertible that stress decreases your sleep. If you are feeling stressed out, you cannot shut up that so called “monkey mind” and will find that you are not going to be able to sleep very well. More so, if you manage stress through drinking alcohol. Many people experience wakefulness after drinking alcohol, though a moderate amount of alcohol will not have this effect, drinking more can build a tolerance which causes **drinkers to wake up within three to four hours**. This effect has everything to do with the effects of alcohol on serotonin conversion into sleep-giving melatonin.

sections.title: How Much Sleep Is Ideal?
sections.text:
After covering the effects which steal our sleep, I should speak to how much sleep is actually recommended. Newborns, of course, need abundant sleep, which abates as we get older. Consult the Graph of ideal sleep below.

The medically recommended amount of sleep is in the dark blue, and shows an acceptable range, with more problematic amounts in light blue. Sadly, most adults report less than the recommended amounts, but as you can see getting less than six hours of sleep will cause serious issues. Older adults, over 65 need less sleep. Still, less than five hours of sleep, and these older adults are going to experience health issues, especially with their immune system.

> **[Graphic]** Chart "Sleep duration recommendations" (National Sleep Foundation, third-party): recommended hours — newborn 0–3 months 14–17; infant 4–11 months 12–15; toddler 1–2 years 11–14; preschool 3–5 years 10–13; school age 6–13 years 9–11; teen 14–17 years 8–10; young adult 18–25 years 7–9; adult 26–64 years 7–9; older adult 65+ 7–8.

sections.title: Sleep and Hormones
sections.text:
How is sleep dictated by hormones? As the graph illustrates, sleep quality is based on the **day/night cycle.** From the graph below, at dawn you will see a purple line representing melatonin dropping off immediately. This is followed by a slight rise of the green line, prolactin, and an immediate raise in the yellow line, which is cortisol. Cortisol, which spikes up as soon as you wake, stimulates dopamine production from the hypothalamus, peaking between 8 and 2, and then falling back down again at the pink sunset of dusk. At this point, melatonin production is stimulated and peaks around three hours later. This is followed by prolactin peaking a little bit. Therefore, what happens when you wake up in the morning is that melatonin drops down in your brain, your hypothalamus becomes really hungry for sugar and so it will stimulate a fight or flight mechanism. This stimulates cortisol production; as you can see from the progression of the yellow line.

> **[Graphic]** Graph "Healthy circadian hormones" (©2016) across dawn, day, dusk and midnight: prolactin and melatonin are high overnight and fall at dawn; cortisol spikes at dawn, with smaller rises around midday and late afternoon, then stays low into the night; dopamine rises after dawn and peaks during the day, falling by dusk; after dusk melatonin and then prolactin climb through the night.

Immediately following cortisol production, **dopamine is released from the hypothalamus**, which allows the system to turn off prolactin. Because Prolactin is what keeps you in a deep deep sleep, that drop in the hormone causes the dream state for which the secondary sleep cycle is famous. This causes the period at the end of the night, right before early morning, where waking up feels impossible. You need a boost in dopamine to be stimulated to actually wake up. We get more cortisol surges in the afternoon, when you eat lunch, than at night. If a person is anxious, their cortisol spikes at night, which is going to suppress melatonin and prolactin production.

sections.title: Melatonin
sections.text:
Go back and revisit the graph above, to review **Melatonin**, a hormone of sleep essential to understanding how stressful sleep affects your immune system. Looking to the image below, you can see the chemical melatonin. Notice that sunlight is the factor that inhibits or prevents melatonin production. Conversely, it is dusk that starts our melatonin production. The image below demonstrates an important point. As the **optic nerve runs right by the red body within the hypothalamus**, it is the hypothalamus that actually sends a message to the **pineal gland,** which then produces the melatonin based off how much light we are getting.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Melatonin": light entering the eye travels along the retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus, which signals the pineal gland; light inhibits melatonin release, darkness allows it. The chemical structure of melatonin is shown.

It is not just sunlight from your eyes that sends these messages, but from your skin as well. One early study (1998) reported that shining light on the back of the knee shifted the body clock — though later studies did not confirm it. Still, I recommend a completely dark room, because even small amounts of light can disturb sleep. To get deep sleep, we must be in a completely dark room. No digital lights, streetlights or even the full moon can be present, or it can adversely affect your sleep. I recommend careful investigation of light in your room, as they will affect the level of melatonin you produce and the depth of your sleep.

> **Light Investigation:**
> - Go into your sleeping room during the night, with the lights off
> - wait for your eyes to adjust, then hunt around for any observable light source.
> - find ways to cover or extinguish the light. Consider blacking out windows with dangling light pollution outside

sections.title: Prolactin
sections.text:
Prolactin is the last Hormone on this chart we should focus on. It is regulated by the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary; dopamine from the hypothalamus switches it off. You may know what prolactin is because it stimulates milk production in pregnant women. In fact, the name of the hormone means pro-lactation. That etymology reflects our understanding when we first discovered prolactin, but it does so much more than producing milk for babies. Prolactin has a role in stimulating milk production in the breast because it manages the immune system. A pregnant or nursing woman needs to make enough antibodies to protect her fetus against the outside world, while feeding the child, and she does that under the influence of prolactin. Prolactin levels are incredibly high during pregnancy. See the image above.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Prolactin": in the hypothalamus, TRH stimulates (+) and dopamine inhibits (−) prolactin release from the anterior pituitary; prolactin acts on the breast and other tissues; suckling feeds back to stimulate more prolactin.

One of the other things that prolactin does for pregnant women is to protect her against the effects of high levels of pregnancy hormones. That is high estrogen, progesterone, and growth hormone; all of which allows the baby to grow rapidly from a little zygote. All these hormones would actually cause a tumor growth in the mother if she did not produce enough prolactin to protect herself. It may be helpful to think of prolactins as metaphorically boxing the ears of the cells, so they do not “hear” the hormones. Prolactin is an important hormone, produced mainly at night in healthy people and produced around the clock in the bodies of pregnant and nursing women. So, while the target tissues for the hormone are up at the breasts, there are other tissues that are targeted by prolactin, and one of them is the **immune system**.

sections.title: Prolactin and the Immune System
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "Prolactin programs the immune system" with a labeled diagram "Organs of the immune system" (National Cancer Institute, third-party): tonsils and adenoids, thymus, lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels, spleen, Peyer's patches, appendix, bone marrow.

As previously stated, prolactin programs your immune system. What does that mean and what is your immune system? We talk about it but what does that look like? Refer to this image above, which outlines the Immune system in the body. Our immune system is made up of multiple different body parts, as well as white blood cells that circulate in the blood system. The most important organ to your immune system is found in the middle of our image, right above your heart: **the thymus**. The thymus is an endocrine gland that produces the hormones which programs white blood cells to know the difference between you and other life. To put it differently, the thymus is responsible for programming white blood cells to target invaders such as viruses, fungus, and bacteria but not your own cells. Now, remember, **Autoimmunity disorder is when your white blood cells have not been programmed accurately**. The thymus is directed in this accuracy by prolactin. While prolactin is high at night, the thymus programs your white blood cells properly. If prolactin is not high at night but high during the day then your thymus does not program your white blood cells accurately, instead those white blood cells will attack you.

Your tonsils and adenoids are on the first line of defense when you breathe in foreign agents. Your **lymph nodes act as a drainage system** for anything that you have breathed in. If the lymph nodes are not overwhelmed, any toxins from the air eventually get drained into their waste disposal system. Your spleen is where the white blood cells dump their chemical programing as well as their collected targets and from these results the spleen then tells your thymus what dangers you have been exposed to and need more protection from. Were I to take a big deep breath and breathe in a cold virus, that virus would first come into contact with the mast cells which are the white blood cells kept in my nasal passages, lungs, and my bronchial tubes. These **mast cells** will immediately collect that information and when they circulate back to the spleen, the spleen will collect the information from those mast cells and tell my Thymus that we have been exposed to the cold virus. The thymus will then send the soldiers out to go after that cold virus, or whatever the infection is, to search and destroy.

> **You Are not Immune From Notes:**
> - Can you name five organs of the Immune system?
> - Can you name three types of Immunity free moving cells?
> - Use the text to update your notes!

Moving on throughout the Immune system: the appendix can be found as a part of your intestine. Its role in the immune system it to actually collect white blood cells. Within the intestine, there are **Peyer's patches** that also act as part of the immune system. Just as your skin and tonsils are collecting information about environmental agents that come into your body, so do your intestine via the appendix and Peyer's patches in the large intestine by collecting information about dangerous elements in your food. These intestinal immune detectors tell the spleen and thymus what they need to fight off, and white blood cells are produced in the bone marrow to do that fighting. The mother cells that produce both white and red blood cells as well as platelets are produced in the bone marrow.

While that is the anatomy of the immune system, refer to the graphic on the left for a look at immunity on the cellular level. You can see all the varieties of white blood cells which operate on two different forms of immunity. The first being **innate immunity,** which means your cells are attaching sensed threats. An example would be macrophages which eat up invaders like pacman, as well as natural killer cells that search out and euthanize cancerous cells. Among the white blood cells are Neutrophils and basophils that go after viruses and bacteria specifically, while eosinophil cells hunt down anything you are allergic to. Now, on to **Adaptive immunity**, the second form of Immunity. You may have heard of these things called T-cells that are programmed to go after specific threats. The **T cells are programmed in the thymus**: the thymus trains white blood cells from the bone marrow into T cells. B cells, a different type of white blood cell, produce antibodies.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram of innate immunity (rapid response — macrophages, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and adaptive immunity (slow response — B cells making antibodies, and T cells, including CD4+ and CD8+ T cells), overlapping at T cells and natural killer T cells.

To outline this, as an example, if you have been exposed to chickenpox you produce **antibodies** programmed to fight chicken pox. So, that next time you get exposed to chickenpox your body is programmed to find and fight it, and you will not contract chicken pox again. Similarly, if you have ever been exposed to the herpes virus, your Thymus will direct the production of antibodies against the herpes virus. Same process if you are exposed to the flu, you will develop antibodies against the flu. If you happen upon Epstein-Barr virus, commonly called mono, you will program T Cells to make antibodies against that virus. Your body remembers what you have been exposed to, as long as your thymus is active. Therefore, If you don't get enough sleep, the thymus cannot do its job in programming T cells. Your body functionally forgets what you have been exposed to so you do not make enough antibodies to fight what you are catching, and your body contracts illnesses you have already defeated before. You should know how to fight this off, but your body cannot act on that knowledge without sleep.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "A balanced immune system": a balanced immune system gives optimal effectiveness. Over-reaction to internal threats causes autoimmune problems (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, type 1 diabetes); over-reaction to external threats causes allergic reactions (food sensitivities, allergies, eczema, asthma, sinusitis). Under-reaction lets cancer develop and allows infections (bacteria, mold/fungus, parasites, viruses). (The original graphic lists hepatitis, HIV, shingles and TB under "cancer.")

A balanced immune system is modeled in the graphic to the right. If you have an external threat, meaning an allergic reaction, your system is having an **overreaction**. On the other hand, an infection indicates that the body **did not react enough**. Your immune system did not react soon enough, so you get an infection. Optimal effectiveness in your immune system means neither infections nor allergic reactions occur. If you have an internal threat, meaning an overreaction on the part of your immune system you are making antibodies to target your healthy bodily function, such as in Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease. An **immunity underreaction** to an internal threat is known as cancer. This is also an aspect of HIV and even shingles falls into that category of immunity maladaptation. Your body has forgotten how to fight off those infections.

Specifically, what does prolactin do for your immunity? It helps to think of prolactin as being protective, but only in the dark, like in the image below. Now, prolactin and your immune system protects you against all toxins, viruses, carcinogens, pollutants, germs, parasites, bacteria, and fungus. Prolactin is constantly on alert in your immune system. All white blood cells are constantly on alert for invasion and are trying to clean house. They do it best in the dark. One way to think about this is if we actually had prolactin high during the day it would be like the soldiers out during the day just shooting everybody, civilians and those who are attacking us. It needs to be done at night when the civilians are sleeping. When the rest of the body is not doing it’s essential functioning it’s actually rejuvenating while the white blood cells are cleaning house and prolactin levels are high. One of the things that **prolactin does is anesthetize the rest of the body** for two reasons. First, to put you into a deep sleep and secondlyso that you do not feel this house cleaning going on. If you have the cancer cells in your breast, you don’t want to feel those macrophages eating that up and prolactin protects you from that.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Prolactin and immunity": a skeleton figure surrounded by threats — viruses, toxins, carcinogens, fungus, pollution, bacteria, germs, parasites — and a shield labeled "Protective prolactin" with a lioness silhouette: nighttime prolactin protects the body.

High daytime prolactin leads to autoimmunity. Think of high daytime prolactin as the lion from the image, woken by its master during the day, it will attack the hand that feeds it. Your own immune system will begin attacking your body, attacking the brain. **Multiple sclerosis** is an autoimmune condition which causes a central nervous disorder, in exactly this way, as does Guillain-Barré syndrome, another autoimmune condition. As previously mentioned; Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Grave’s disease, hyperthyroidism are all autoimmune conditions. Certain blood disorders, such as lupus and hemolytic anemias are autoimmune conditions. Some GI disorders; like celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, and colitis are all autoimmune attacks on your intestine. Then we have nerve disorders, like peripheral neuropathy, as well as multiple schlerosis, both of which are attacks on our own nervous system. There are some kinds of granulomatous diseases, where your lungs actually become stiffened and your body is attacking your own lungs. This disease is very uncommon, but nevertheless it is also an autoimmune disease.

Autoimmune disease can be quite visible. **Vitiligo** of the skin, when your skin loses color, is what Michael Jackson suffered from. He lost the coloration of his skin from vitiligo, an autoimmune condition where the body attacks the melanin colorants in the skin. Eczema, psoriasis, and scleroderma are all other forms of autoimmune disease where the skin becomes quite tight and thick like an alligator’s skin. As previously mentioned, fibromyalgia and multiple sclerosis are also autoimmune diseases. When the immune system attacks our bones we will see rheumatoid arthritis and polymyalgia rheumatic, an overall arthritis that is not rheumatoid. Ankylosing spondylitis, where the bones of the vertebrae become incredibly painful, is an attack on our own vertebrae. In these conditions, the bones are being deconstructed cell by cell.

So, if your immune system is not protecting you, it may be attacking you and that is what we have to stop. The simplest way to stop and prevent these many conditions is to **change the circadian rhythm**. Normalizing the sleep cycle, building prolactin only at night for protection, and low prolactin during the day will produce enough dopamine to turn prolactin off. It is important to have normal adrenal function, so the body does not stimulate cortisol in the middle of the night, instead stimulating prolactin in the middle of the night. Anything we can do to try to sleep deeper is critical to keeping these hormones in balance.

sections.title: Healthy Sleep Habits
sections.text:
Let us focus on the best sleep habits. We have two ways of dealing with sleep: the first is useful after dusk and the second helps once we get into the bed. Here is what I recommend after it becomes dark, condition your light intake, that pink and low light of dusk being incredibly important to inducing sleep. If you are exposed to the blue light of a television screen, computer screen, smartphone screen, or tablet screen, you are signalling to your pineal gland via the hypothalamus that the sun in fact did not go down. Therefore, you will not make melatonin soon enough to actually get deep sleep, and in fact you will not make prolactin in an adequate amount of time either. This pushes prolactin’s period of increase into the daytime instead of the night time.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Normalize your sleep cycle": the healthy circadian hormone graph (cortisol spike at dawn, dopamine peaking by day, melatonin and prolactin rising after dusk through the night) with the "Protective prolactin" shield.

For this, **tinted sunglasses** can help, with lenses of either pink, red, deep amber, or orange will all work. These colorful spectacles block daytime-signaling blue rays from your vision receptors. However, this does nothing for skin sensitivity. These sunset-tinted light blockers signal to your pineal gland, that the sun went down, it is night time, and it is time to start making melatonin. Normally, it takes about three hours after dusk for you to peak in your melatonin production, which is why you feel sleepy pretty quickly when you are camping. Three hours have passed from sunset and you are ready to go to bed, because you are making enough melatonin to sleep.

**Do not try to stimulate your wakefulness** after dark. Do not engage in mentally exciting activities, keep as calm as possible. Just as with putting little children to bed: if you get them all riled up, it is impossible to get them to sleep. Well, the same principle applies to adults: If you get yourself all excited, perhaps you are watching some dynamic television show that interests or frightens you, it is going to be hard to fall asleep. Getting into arguments before going to bed is also not conducive to deep sleep. I recommend trying to **eat dinner early**. If you are concerned about going to bed on an empty stomach, a very light snack like nut butters on whole grain crackers will help stabilize your blood sugar.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Best sleep habits." After dusk: no blue light; pink (blue-blocking) sunglasses for TV; keep calm, no stimulation after dark; eat dinner early; limit alcohol to avoid rebound awakening. Once in bed: completely dark room; soothing sounds; cool room temperature; warm bed; contraction/relaxation exercises.

White noise can help you fall asleep and stay asleep. Although everybody has a different sound that calms them, but those monotonous sounds especially nature sounds like waves will actually calm you. Soothing sounds calm the brain chemistry. Soothed brain chemistry produces higher levels of melatonin and prolactin at night. Moreover your room should be cool and if you are running a heater in your room and the room gets too hot, you will wake up. That does not mean you cannot be nice and cozy under the covers, but the **room temperature itself should be cool**. Therefore, if you overheat, your subliminal mind will have you kick off the covers. If you have a heater running at night, it’s going to keep the room temperature too hot and you will not sleep deeply enough.

> **Sleep Hygiene Exercise:**
> - Take note of each of the Best Sleep Habits you use
> - Write down each sleep habit you have which counters a Best Sleep Habit
> - What changes need to be made to maximize your sleep?

I want to touch on some **contraction and relaxation exercises** that are good for sleep. Studies on menopausal women who wake up in the middle of the night with hot flashes found that subjects who performed contraction and relaxation exercises to reset their body before sleep were less likely to wake up in the middle of the night. These exercises consist of a conscious contraction from the toes all the way up to the neck and head. Contract each part of your body in turn, holding it for just a second or two, and then slowly relax the muscles. Repeat this from the feet to the head and repeat the process three times. This works to burn off excess adrenaline, helping you exit that fight or flight mode. Lowering your adrenaline also relaxes the body, by helping your body produce more GABA, which has a relaxing effect. Finally, you can go to sleep.

sections.title: Exercise to Support Sleep
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "3) Physical activity for best sleep": exercise early in the day; avoid aerobic or strenuous exercise after dark; relaxing forms of yoga are OK.

How else can physical activity give you your best sleep? To support a healthy circadian rhythm, your body needs **exercise early** in the day while avoiding aerobic and strenuous exercise after dark. More relaxing forms of exercise, like yoga, are fine. But if you are going to exercise very strenuously after dark, you will raise your cortisol level while suppressing your melatonin levels. My patients who must sit throughout work and then exercise afterwards find that they cannot sleep. So, it is super important that we exercise early in the day- **But right before bed, avoiding strenuous exercise** in favor of more relaxing activities. For a healthy immune system you must partake in aerobic exercise, at least three times a week. In the daytime, preferably outside, just move and be active, while recovering between bouts of exercise with gentle stretching and yoga. It is essential to the immune system’s adoption of normal day/night cycles that we move the body, moving the immune system’s lymph organs requires muscles be moving. Yoga and stretching is good for that as well, but we must get the oxygen going, and thus breathing hard.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "3) Physical activity for optimal immune function": aerobic exercise 3 times a week; recover in between with gentle stretching or yoga; get outside and be active — just move!

Do you already exercise, and how can we be sure be sure it is effective? So, one way to assess aerobic capacity is through the breath. If you are taking a brisk walk, perhaps you are going up a hill with a friend. Before you get to the hill, you may notice you can chat easily, but then you have trouble talking as you go up the hill. This is due to aerobic capacity. When you get to the point where you cannot talk and do the activity at the same time, your activity has reached an aerobic level. That is the aerobic level I recommend for your early morning exercise, for getting the heart rate up. You will recover greater talking/breathing ability as you get more fit, but generally it is better to use this chatting test while exercising instead of stopping to take your pulse. What I do when exercising alone is to start singing to myself. If I cannot sing, then I know I am at aerobic capacity.

If they are going to bed after midnight and yet they have to get up between six and eight AM, then these patients are probably not getting enough sleep and they are definitely making prolactin during the day. Such people need to go to bed earlier, and this can be done despite great difficulty by gradually moving your bedtime back by fifteen minutes every night. The goal is to get into bed within three hours of dusk. During the winter time we all need more sleep.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "4) Sleep for optimal immune function": a woman sleeping in a dark room and the "Protective prolactin" shield — deep sleep in darkness lets nighttime prolactin program immunity.

If you miss that longer winter sleep, what is going to happen when spring rolls around is that your adrenals are not going to kick in and you are going to suffer **adrenal fatigue**. We progress into spring rather abruptly, giving Californians a tendency towards adrenal dysfunction, especially adrenal fatigue. These conditions need support from Winter solstice through midwinter, around December 21st to about February 1st. These people need extra adrenal support because our spring can start in January. Daffodils are blooming, and the adrenals are trying to kick in to spring fever. To make this transition, they need sleep during the winter. The Adrenals did not get that long winter rest they needed to actually rejuvenate themselves.

So be sure you are definitely sleeping longer in the Winter then in the Summer time you can sleep in a little bit, as you do not need as much sleep because the days are longer. It is really hard to go to sleep at ten o’clock at night when it does not become dark until nine. You are probably not going to be able to go to sleep until midnight, but that is okay in summer time. It just should not be your habit all year long.

Stress is one of the biggest issues that affect people’s health. If you look to the Image on the right, you will see how stress affects our bodies. Stress affects diverse systems in our body. As we become more stressed, our thinking is more labored with trouble concentrating, rising depression and anxiety. An affected person may feel a “brain throb”, this is stress affecting the cardiovascular system. When you are under stress, your heart races, you experience palpitations, you may even have increased blood pressure or an increased risk for a heart attack and stroke. Stress can give us achiness in our muscles and joints, caused by inflammation all over the body. The immune system does not function very well under stress, which is why we can fall ill after being stressed. You may find that you catch colds and flus that you do not normally catch. Illness itself may become a major stressor, creating a vicious cycle.

The deeply stressed can even come down with cancers. Stresses’ detriment to the immune system is truly astounding. Long-term stress can lead to changes in the skin and hair, such as brittleness, dryness, or even loss of hair. I have had patients who have become completely bald due to stressors; stress-induced alopecia. The effects cannot be understated. Acne is a widely known effect of stress, many will break out with rashes or acne when stressed. Studies have shown that if you are under stress and you recently had an injury or surgery, it is less likely they heal properly.

> **Stress Test:**
> - Pop Quiz: list your ten biggest stressors
> - You can be as candid as you want in your own notes, free write instinctually.
> - Note you reactions to reading each item. Are you surprised? Exhausted?

Additionally, the gut cannot absorb or digest nutrients properly while stressed. There is a term in Italian called “agita”, which translates as “acid stomach”, but colloquially refers to being so anxious that you cannot eat properly. Of course, anxiety also affects the reproductive system. One of the interesting things about stress is that it can delay your ability to become fertile by lowering sperm count and interfering with ovulation. It is a classic story that when a couple finally decides to adopt they become pregnant after the peace of signing the adoption papers. Stress can really affect you and affect all parts of your body. In this document we are going to explore the main organ that controls your stress response and how you can handle your stress in a way that creates health and well being.

So what stresses our body? The three main things that stress you are

- eating too much sugar

> **[Graphic]** Slide "What stresses your body": too much sugar, overwork and constant demands, and screens in bed at night.

- not sleeping in the dark

- being over exposed to blue lights

Those are the main things that you can really control. You can also control your stress response, which is depicted in the image to the right by this gentleman being overwhelmed with his computer and all these rigid memos. It is important to know that what could be stressful for one person is not necessarily stressful for another, and so perception defines the stress. That which stresses your body is generally under your control, according to how you respond to your stress. So we do know that stress is caused by happy and sad major life changes such as marriage, birth, divorce and death. But stress is not only caused by big changes such as going to college, leaving home, or moving; but also by everyday stressors such as arguments, relationships, work events, financial responsibilities or living with chronic illness.

> **[Graphic]** Graphic "Major life changes + everyday stressors = STRESS!": perfectionism, relationships, work, money, past trauma, worried attitude, illness.

But these stressors are shaped by our mindset. Medical professionals know that people with a perfectionist attitude tend to perceive life as stressful because such effort is ever quite satisfying. Pessimists are also constantly worried as they see their glass being half empty rather than half full. We also have noted that past traumas dictate the way that your body actually reacts to stress, both the way you react to stress in the central nervous system as well the way your adrenals react to stress. In my practice, I call it the “Chihuahua response” rather than the “bloodhound response”. Instead of being relaxed about their surroundings and only getting up and dealing with things that are necessary, to the patient with a “chihuahua response”, everything is a stressor. All of these factors can be shifted in favor of your health. We cannot control what is happening outside of us, but we can shift how we perceive these events and we can shift our biochemistry.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram of the stress (HPA) axis: the hypothalamus releases CRH → the pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal glands (on top of the kidneys) release cortisol and adrenaline. Acute stress (fight-or-flight) enhances the immune system, memory, energy replenishment and cardiovascular function; chronic stress suppresses the immune system and memory and promotes bone mineral loss, muscle wasting and metabolic syndrome.

sections.title: The Biology of Stress
sections.caution: The POMC description in this section is being revised by Deborah. Do not state that CRH, TRH or GRF are made from POMC.
sections.text:
So let us look at what’s going on in the brain, refer to the Image below. There are two aspects of stress: You have an **acute stress response** and **chronic stress response**.

- The Acute Stress Response-refers to momentary stress, the fight or flight response, created by our **adrenal glands**. You may experience this response when you get excited by something; no matter what it is. Perhaps you get stressed out by being in the car, or perhaps it is made worse when you are late to go somewhere. You may have bills that you suddenly remember. Any particular aspect of stress is going to cause that response because your hypothalamus does not know the difference between these everyday stressors and a tiger chasing you, so the stress response given by your endocrine system is exactly the same. Your reaction to that stressor starts the fight or flight response, so your adrenal glands give forth the **adrenaline** that allows your body to actually mobilize to get away or struggle to fight off the stressor. Once the adrenaline is produced, your body starts producing cortisol in order to release stored sugar from your liver and your muscles to give you the necessary fuel to get away from that danger or fight that danger. You may notice that while this chemical reaction is happening everything is enhanced, sensory information is heightened, and your memory is better. All to aid in your escape. So too is your immune system acutely heightened. Throughout these sensations your body is mobilizing energy from your storage and your cardiovascular function is at peak performance for survival, but that doesn’t last very long.

- In chronic stress, you have the same response detailed above but it never turns off. So your adrenal glands become **incredibly fatigued by chronically producing these stress hormones,** adrenaline and cortisol, which creates a deficiency in these hormones over time. Eventually, your overactive immune system is suppressed, your overused memory is not as good, and you actually start losing muscle and bone tissue. This is because the stress hormone cortisol is **catabolic**; its eats away at your tissues. This destructive act is meant to mobilize energy stores, but when those energy stores are depleted from your muscles and liver, cortisol starts eating away at other tissues. In the beginning of this chronic stress reaction, stress causes you to lose weight, but eventually you will start gaining weight.

In the illustration below you can see the **hypothalamus** and pituitary **glands**, and both creating this feedback mechanism between the brain and the adrenals.

Let us look a little bit deeper into this process. Now, in the graphic to the left, (which was drawn for my book, ‘**Hormones in Harmony’** by my daughter) you can see why stress affects all the other organs in the body. **POMC** is one of the stress response hormones produced in the hypothalamus. POMC triggers the cortical releasing hormones in the adrenals and thyroid via the pituitary. That specific hormone which affects the adrenals is called **adrenocorticotropic hormone** and its job is to get the adrenals to produce cortisol, but the one hormone that creates this little feedback mechanism, POMC, also controls the thyroid. Specifically, POMC controls how the liver stores glucose and whether or not the pancreas produces insulin and glucagon. POMC also controls the melanocyte-stimulating hormone which actually controls your day-night cycles, and then what is left over from the Hypothalamus’ POMC becomes beta-endorphins. As you can see, stressors affect far more than simply the adrenals. Stressors also affect thyroid function, glucose function, day-night cycles, and your level of happiness.

The image to the right is a depiction of your adrenals, which are pretty amazing organs. Often mentioned are their production of adrenaline and cortisol, but there are so many more hormones made by the adrenals. After all, the adrenals are endocrine glands so they produce hormones and release some via the bloodstream. However, the adrenals are stimulated not just by the endocrine response, which is the **hypothalamic pituitary adrenal Axis**, but are also stimulated by a nerve response. It is the nerve response (refer to the image depicting the neuronal response) that actually stimulates adrenaline. This entry is not controlled by the hypothalamus, but is a nervous system reaction.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Your adrenals — adrenal gland" (©2016): the medulla makes adrenaline (autonomic nervous system); the cortex has three zones — reticular zone makes DHEA (anabolic steroids; protein and fat metabolism), fascicular zone makes cortisol (glucocorticoids; glucose metabolism), glomerular zone makes aldosterone (mineralocorticoids; salt/water balance). The gland is regulated by neuronal, hormonal and humoral signals.

The **neuronal response** is a reaction that is learned and deeply encoded by experience as well as the experience of our genetic ancestors. For instance, almost every human has a fear response to snakes as we have learned that they are dangerous and that advantage was encoded into our systems. As the recipients of this inherited advantage, we do not need to think when simply seeing something on the ground that is reminiscent of a snake because most people automatically pull back from it and don’t go further until they feel assured of safety. This is a protective response. Along with this nerve stimulated adrenaline, the adrenals do create the hormonal response. The hormonal response received by the adrenals is caused by the hypothalamus and pituitary stimulating cortisol production and, in that case, both cortisol and DHEA are produced.

> **Nervous or Nerve-you?**
> - Go over your list of stressors
> - Check off each Stressor rooted in a cause from memory

> - These starred stressors may be better thought of as inherited through instinct.

**Cortisol** is a catabolic glucocorticoid steroid and actually controls how you metabolize sugar. Cortisol dissolves tissues while **DHEA**, which is an anabolic steroid, builds tissue up. DHEA also helps you metabolize protein and fat, so the two go together. DHEA follows cortisol, and cortisol always rises first in a system while it makes enough DHEA. Why? To repair any damage caused by Cortisol during the fight or flight response.

At the very surface of the adrenal gland, which is cyclically bathed in blood, lies the system of the humoral response. This bloodstream medium is actually giving messages to the adrenal glands, such as to begin adjusting blood pressure with a hormone called **aldosterone** which controls how much salt and water balance within the bloodstream. The adrenals talk to your kidneys through the humoral response as well. Not covered in our image, are the adrenal produced met-enkephalins, which help to control your immune system. The adrenals do a lot for your health and they are rather unappreciated. We only pay attention to them when they get fatigued and while they are keeping us alive all of the time.

sections.title: Adrenal Dis-Ease — Signs of Adrenal Fatigue
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "Signs of adrenal fatigue": exhaustion (wired but tired, crash in the afternoon); inability to sleep through the night; cravings (salt, fat, sugar); weight gain around the middle; hair loss; irregular periods; low libido; mood swings (depression, anxiety, no motivation).

So what are the signs of adrenal fatigue? To the left is a short list graphic. We have already touched on what would render a patient’s adrenals fatigued: Chronic Stress. If a person has been under stress for a long period of time, they will find that their adrenals are not producing as much hormone as they should be. Such a patient will notice a normalized level of exhaustion. This fatigue is a little different from normal exhaustion however. The patient may be fatigued all day, but typically they crash in the afternoon. For instance, when they wake up in the morning they might feel pretty good, but between one and five o’clock; usually around three o’clock, they have an energy crash. They crave sugar and caffeine to try to return that energy. Or they may have a sense of being exceptionally tired but underneath the surface feeling a little wired. They may feel a little frenetic energy because the adrenaline is still surging. Without cortisol to fuel the fight or flight reaction, the panic comes out as that “Chihuahua” shaking.

The patient will have trouble sleeping through the night, and not only because of this wired-tired feeling. You see, often times when people have adrenal fatigue they produce too much cortisol at night and not enough during the day. They also have cravings for sugar, fat, and salt. Usually sugar is desired primarily, then salt and fat in that order. People’s weight tends to accumulate around their middle with chronic adrenal fatigue. The hypothalamus believes their person has been chased up a tree by a tiger and they may not be able to get a meal. The patient will notice hair loss, usually on their head, and followed by body-hair loss over time. The classic signs of low DHEA in the middle-aged person is the loss of secondary sexual characteristics in terms of body hair and women’s periods will become irregular. Adrenal fatigue sufferers of all genders will have a low libido, mood swings, depression and anxiety. Suffers do not have much motivation and they may perceive events and obligations as much bigger than they actually are. They may feel as if they are always facing mountains of responsibility; everything is just too big for them to handle.

sections.title: Adrenal Stress and Insulin Resistance
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Adrenal stress leads to insulin resistance — the stress response" (©2016): a stressor acts on the hypothalamus → pituitary → adrenal. The adrenal releases adrenaline (raises heart rate), aldosterone (raises blood pressure), cortisol and DHEA (repairs tissue). Cortisol converts to cortisone (shown next to inflammation) and drives the pancreas: glucagon releases stored sugar and insulin moves it into cells to fuel fight-or-flight. Repeated over time, this pushes toward insulin resistance.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Insulin receptor — effects of insulin" (©2016): when insulin binds its receptor on the cell membrane, glucose transporters open entry for glucose, amino acids and free fatty acids, drives glycolysis/oxidation (energy) and triglyceride storage, and switches off gluconeogenesis (making new sugar).

Adrenal stress eventually leads to insulin resistance. Why would that be? Well, during the stress response, the hypothalamus hormonally causes the pituitary gland to trigger the adrenals to release cortisol. As adrenaline is released first, your heart rate speeds up and **aldosterone** is released to raise your blood pressure. Cortisol begins releasing stored sugar, which releases glucagon from the pancreas, and then the body begins breaking down the sugar. Then the pancreas releases insulin to make use of the sugar. When cortisol has done its job it becomes **cortisone**, which is found in cortisone creams sold to rub on rashes. It should not surprise you to find that cortisone is a natural anti-inflammatory. So, cortisone is released in response to the inflammation which breaks out when the stored sugars are broken down. The body then produces DHEA, which starts to repair the tissue from which the sugar was ripped. This cascade of hormones: adrenaline, aldosterone, cortisol and DHEA occurs in response to the stressor.

This cascade, occurring over time, leads to insulin resistance. What happens with insulin resistance? What does that actually mean? Please look below, where you will see one of my favorite graphics. This is the insulin receptor in the cell membrane, which are the green and yellow structures. I find that the image looks to me like a butter sandwich where you’ve got the bread. In actuality, the butter and bread are glycoproteins ( sugar protein) and phospholipids (fats). All this makes up the cell wall. Between that, we have the receptor sites that allow hormones to get into the cells. This “R-Triangle” is situated around the receptor site that allows insulin into the cell through activated gateways or portals. Insulin binds its receptor (the R triangle), which signals glucose transporters (GLUT4) to let glucose into the cell. Once insulin is bound, the portals through which we see substances entering the cell open.

These portals:

1\) allow glucose into the cell

2\) allow amino acids into the cell

3\) allow fatty acids into the cell and it also allows water in and out of the cell.

So if you by chance develop insulin resistance, then these receptor sites are not allowing insulin and sugar to lock in and be processed by the cell for energy. That is what glucose is about, providing energy for your body. As amino acids, fatty acid, or water are subsequently also not allowed into your cells these cells will starve. Becoming insulin resistant is not just about going without sugar, but suffering malnutrition and dehydration as well.

The above graphic also shows us that a lack of glucose coming into the cell will cause the cell to fabricate glucose from available protein and fat. However, if you have too much glucose coming in, glucose stimulates triglyceride production through glycolysis, and those triglycerides are stored in fat cells. An incredibly efficient system, yet a system that can become blocked to great detriment

sections.title: Causes of Insulin Resistance
sections.text:
Now, why would a person become insulin resistant? Well, if the body is not really using the chemical energy provided to get away from that tiger, it will eventually need to store it somewhere. Insulin resistance is a way your body saves itself from causing too much damage. After all, insulin and glucose are incredibly inflammatory so excesses of both in a system can cause damage to the arteries, heart, and other tissues. To handle this, those tissues learn how to become resistant to insulin by blocking insulin's access to the cell, especially the life-critical heart.

Your heart muscles is about as big as your fist. If you make a fist and place it over your heart then you can approximate its size. If the heart grows any larger than that, this is diagnosed as cardiomegaly. Such a heart is actually too big for the body and will not be an efficient pump. Normally, the only thing your heart can do with that extra glucose is beat faster or grow. The heart knows it is not supposed to grow any larger, so it will eventually block excess insulin from getting into heart cells. This is a manifestation of insulin resistance, which leads to the extra sugar being stored as triglycerides in your fat. Remember that particular fat is stored around your belly, like a guardian. The fat is stored there to help you, to protect your vital organs.

sections.text:
My recommendation to check for adrenal dysfunction is a blood test. Before that test, is the simple matter of taking blood pressure. You can check your blood pressure yourself or with a friend whom you can pay back by offering to check their blood pressure afterward. To introduce you to the test, first I want you to imagine that you are lying underneath a tree relaxing after a nap. Then all of a sudden, a predator like a tiger approaches to eat you! If you cannot jump and run away, such as if your blood pressure bottoms out, you are going to become the tiger’s dinner. So you should have a blood pressure that rises at least 10 to 20 points from the prone position to the upright position. To simulate this, we have you lie down for a few minutes and we measure your blood pressure after you have been lying down. We then immediately stand you up and measure your blood pressure again. If your pressure does not rise 10 to 20 points then that is a sign of adrenal aldosterone dysfunction. To explain, if your body is not producing enough **aldosterone** then you do not produce enough cortisol for that stress response nor enough DHEA to get away from a tiger.

For our next test, keep in mind that one of the things that we crave when we are under stress and our adrenals are fatigued, is salt. The reason we crave salt is because our aldosterone is being wasted and we will later be urinating out quite a bit of salt. We become very dehydrated when we do not have enough salt in our system. By salt, I’m not just referring to iodized salt or that from processed foods, I am actually referring to about sea salt. Why sea salt? Because this naturally occurring salt has all the minerals that your body needs in order to stay healthy.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "BP test for adrenal dysfunction": lie down for a few minutes; measure blood pressure lying down; immediately stand up and measure again. Blood pressure should rise 10–20 points, both systolic and diastolic; if it doesn't, Deborah reads it as a sign of adrenal aldosterone dysfunction.

Let us get into the salt hydration test. If a patient says they are drinking noticeable amounts of water and they never feel hydrated, I will have them perform a **Salt-Hydration** test by having them put two teaspoons of salt in a finger bowl, such as in the image below, and having them eat the salt throughout their day until they cannot stand to eat one more grain. Then I have them measure how much salt is left in the bowl and subtract that from the original two teaspoons. If you consumed one teaspoon of salt, that is how much salt you need for the day. As a secondary test, I have them keep track of how much water they drank that day. Most people need about one ounce of water per kilogram of body weight (or half ounce of water per pound of body weight). I find that most people who eat well, not the standard American diet, do not get enough salt as they tend to cut salt out of their diet and so they become dehydrated. Adding a little bit of salt back into the diet will make a big difference to a person’s hydration.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Sea salt for adrenal health — salt hydration test": pour 2 teaspoons of sea salt into a small bowl; eat the salt throughout the day until you can't stand one more grain; measure how much is left and subtract from the original 2 tsp (2 tsp − amount left = daily need); also track how much water you need to satisfy your thirst.

sections.title: Lab Tests
sections.text:
So what lab tests do I use to test for adrenal dysfunction and to test for insulin resistance? For adrenal dysfunction, I investigate **DHEA-S**, the sulfated (conjugated) form of DHEA, which is the stable circulating reservoir of the hormone. If the DHEA-S count is low, the patient has adrenal fatigue. If the count is high, the patient is under acute stress and they probably have metabolic syndrome. Remember the heart issues? They can also affect these tests: high blood pressure, being overweight, high cholesterol, or even polycystic ovary syndrome all lead to high DHEA levels. Testing plain DHEA, in its unconjugated form, measures the shorter-lived active hormone. The only time we can truly measure this value is first thing in the morning.

Time also matters in test on cortisol, if cortisol is very low in the morning, in a blood test that can be a sign of low adrenals in the patient. Now the problem with measuring cortisol is that **cortisol is going to spike** a little bit at any sign of possible danger, such as the white coat of the health care provider or the needle they are carrying. So such a test will not always get an accurate result, which has led me to measure DHEA-S to investigate the adrenals.

Now insulin resistance, I investigate that through **hemoglobin A1c**. Hemoglobin A1c is a measurement of a protein found on your red blood cells, actually within the hemoglobin of the red blood cells. If this value is measured over 5.6%, then you may have insulin resistance. If the patient’s hemoglobin A1c is 6.5% or higher, that indicates type 2 diabetes; 5.7–6.4% is prediabetes. I could also test for **C-peptide**. The body produces insulin from a larger protein molecule called proinsulin. When proinsulin splits apart, it releases one molecule of insulin and one molecule of C-peptide in equal amounts. Insulin breaks down very quickly in the liver, but C-peptide stays in the bloodstream longer, making it a reliable marker of how hard your beta cells are working. If C-peptide is measured to be over 3.5 ng/ml, the patient has insulin resistance. While a c-peptide of less than 0.1 ng/ml indicates type 1 diabetes, as the body is not producing enough insulin. If the **triglycerides** are elevated over 100 mg/dl, the body is probably insulin resistant. If the **LDL subparticle** is in pattern B (pattern A being healthiest) then the body is making too many small particles, which leads to insulin resistance. We have many options in testing insulin resistance via the blood.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Lab tests." Adrenal dysfunction: DHEA-S, the stable circulating reservoir (low = adrenal fatigue; high = acute stress or metabolic syndrome); DHEA; cortisol low in the morning. Insulin resistance: HbA1c above 5.6 (6.5% or higher indicates type 2 diabetes); C-peptide above 3.5 (below 0.1 = type 1 diabetes); triglycerides above 100; LDL subparticle pattern B.

sections.title: Five Pillars of Healthy Hormones
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Graphic "5 Pillars of Healthy Hormones": Balance your Hypothalamus, Healthy Nutrition, Adequate Exercise, Restorative Sleep, Healing Mindset.

The Five Pillars of Healthy Hormones in adrenal hormones and healthy insulin production requires that we balance the hypothalamus, take in proper nutrition, get adequate activity, become restored with healthy sleep, and implement healing mindsets. Let us get right into it.

Supporting your hypothalamus for a healthy stress response **restores optimal hypothalamic function and balances the HPA axis**. [Genesis Gold](https://genesisgold.com/genesisgold/) is for that exactly, promoting “healthy adrenal function”. That is what Genesis Gold does. I made it myself so that I would not have to give my patients so many different bottles of hormonal support. By taking Genesis Gold, you can support your body through the uncomfortable stress response.

One of the biggest stressors that I recently underwent was the death of my mother in 2015. Helping her through her terminal illness for seven months was incredibly stressful. The experience dramatically affected my hormones. But one thing the ongoing tragedy did not affect was my health. I did not become ill and I did not crash. In fact, I was able to function during this difficult time. If my three sisters were also taking Genesis Gold during this time; I truly believe they would have made it through the crisis healthier, with less ageing effects, increased energy and well being to function.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "1) Support your hypothalamus for a healthy stress response" with a jar of Genesis Gold. The goals Deborah lists: restore optimal hypothalamic function, balance the HPA axis, support healthy adrenal function, help reverse insulin resistance at the cellular level.

Stress will age you by breaking down your tissues. Stress hurts your body and causes disease. So balancing your body out on a regular basis can make a huge difference to your health. However, there is another aspect to healing the stress response, which is to reverse that **insulin resistance**. We must get the insulin into the cells, use your sugar appropriately, and stop storing excess weight around your middle. At 58 years old I get comments on my stomach quite a bit because I still have a very slender waist. The reason for that is because I never developed insulin resistance, even through my middle age. I feel assured that this is due to supporting my body with Genesis Gold. My patients on Genesis Gold for the long term, such as my patients in their 80s, generally do not have the age-related insulin resistance that is so common.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "2) Nutrition for a healthy stress response": limit sugar and processed foods; colorful fruits and vegetables; adequate fat; sea salt. Photo of whole foods — vegetables, fruit, eggs, poultry, meat and fish.

Moving on to the other side of this process, the diet. What is the nutrition recommended for a healthy stress response? We are once more going to need an almost **Paleo diet**. We must get an adequate amount of protein, healthy fats, as well as plentiful colorful fruits and vegetables. We cannot forget to limit how much starch and sugar, especially those from processed foods. Lastly, we add sea salt. The basic Mediterranean type diet with its pasta grains are included, as long as they are whole grains. It is important to limit the amount of active carbohydrates you are ingesting, compared to the amount you are burning off.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "2) Insulin Resistant Diet" showing a plate divided into 40% carbohydrates (fruits and vegetables), 30% protein and 30% fat: lots of colorful fruits and vegetables; enough protein and enough fat for your lean body mass; limit starchy carbs and sugars (the slide misspells "starchy" as "Stacy").

Now, for the **insulin-resistant diet**, which I think of as a “30-30-40 plan”. It is similar to The Zone diet (40% carbohydrate, 30% protein, 30% fat); Atkins, by contrast, is a low-carbohydrate diet. This plan is easy to implement by visualizing your plate. Referring to our image above, 40% of your plate should be covered by carbohydrates, 30% would be covered in protein, and 30% would be fat. Remember that fat has nine calories per gram, so you are not going to have one-third of the plate here in fat, it would be half of that, calorically. Visually, however 30% would be fat. Included in carbohydrates are lots of colorful fruits and vegetables. You need half a gram to one gram of protein per pound of lean body mass. While fat is more one size fits all, most people should have no more than half a gram of fat for your lean body mass. Finally, limit the starchy carbs and sugars.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "3) Physical activity for optimal health": HIIT exercise 3 times a week; recover in between with gentle stretching or yoga; get outside and be active — just move!

Of course, there needs to be **physical activity** for optimal health. I recommend HIT exercises three times a week. Recover in between these trainings with gentle stretching and yoga, but be sure that you are not exercising too late. If you exercise after dark, you are going to stimulate a cortisol response; consequently, you are not going to sleep as well. After dark you can do yoga and stretch. You can do gentle things, but not aerobic activity. Morning and afternoon are great times to get outside and be active because it stimulates a healthy cortisol response and also helps to reduce insulin resistance. The main thing is that we must move, just get up and move around. It can be helpful to get a sit-stand desk, and stand more while sitting less. I have found that moving just ten minutes three times a day, is better than nothing.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "4) Sleep for optimal immune function": get enough sleep for your age; sleep in the dark; wake up with the sun.

Even that low amount of movement will help to reduce your insulin resistance, if you are getting **enough quality sleep for optimal immune response**. We have to get enough sleep in complete darkness so that we can wake up with the sun. This helps us reset our healthy cortisol response, to reset a healthy adrenal response, and to reverse insulin resistance. You cannot achieve this without sleeping in the dark.

Finally, the **healing mindse**t for healthy immunity, healthy adrenal response, and healthy immune response requires **calm**. Calm is what I teach to my patients. Calm is connecting with your breath, calm is attitude, calm is love, and calm is meditation. As an example, when I am dealing with a stressor the first thing I do is I take a deep breath. I connect as I breathe, and by connection I mean that I am just becoming conscious with my breath. What happens when people are under stress is that they hyperventilate. So, as an opposite, take in as deep a breath as you can and exhale slowly. You’ll notice that you will be able to think more clearly as you get more oxygen. Then you can instantaneously adopt a positive attitude in that moment. People have a knee-jerk reaction to stressors, in that they either immediately see it as an obstacle or an opportunity. It’s difficult to see something that appears as a stressor to be an opportunity. It is easier to see it as an obstacle because it’s almost a trained response.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "5) Healing mindset for healthy immunity — CALM": Connect (with breath); Attitude (opportunity, not obstacle); Love (as the lens of perception); Meditation (with scent and sound). Photo of a woman meditating by the sea.

So I want you to start looking at your stressors as a potential opportunity. Then I want you to focus on perceiving through the lenses of love, rather than fear. This can mean sitting with that knee-jerk reaction of fear, just enough to start to feel grateful and have a little compassion for the situation. If you have compassion for yourself in dealing with the stressor then you will start seeing stressors not just as scary but more of an opportunity. Things will become more relaxed. Practicing that meditation with sound and fragrance makes a huge difference in your ability to induce this biochemical reaction. You will reverse the fear response if you practice with scent and sound. Just using that smell, you know what that calming smell can do, will help you to calm down. I smell my grandmother’s coffee and I think of her peace between hectic work and then I quickly relax.

> **Reset the Mind:**
> - Refer back to your list of Stressors
> - How could each provide you an environment in which to develop yourself?
> - How could each gift you with a new perspective?
> - What does each irritant help you understand about yourself?

If you practice daily meditation with scent and a relaxing soothing sound then it will be much easier to connect with your breath to attain an attitude that this stressor is an opportunity instead of an obstacle. Doing this daily makes it easier to perceive your life through lenses of love rather than through fear. So, remember the Five Pillars: balance your hypothalamus, eat a healthy diet, get adequate exercise, take restorative sleep, and have a healing mindset. Thank you for your time. I want you to know, lastly, that you can calm your stress response with Genesis Gold. I wish you well.

Many patients who are concerned about their weight focus on the role their thyroid plays in our metabolism. They blame their thyroid for their sense of energy, and there is some truth to that association; however, the thyroid affects far more than just weight and energy production. Referring to the image above, the thyroid affects:

- The cardiovascular system

- Digestion and gut health

- Reproduction, in both males and females

- The bones.

- Our skin and hair

- Last, but not least, the brain.

> **[Graphic]** Diagram "Hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis" (©2016): hypothalamic POMC leads to TRH → the pituitary releases TSH → the thyroid (using iodine and the enzyme TPO) makes T4, which converts to active T3 or inactive reverse T3 (rT3). T4/T3 and TSH balance like a seesaw — when thyroid hormone is low, TSH rises.

Because the thyroid affects so many parts of the body, this document focuses on the thyroid and its effect on the rest of your hormones.

To the left you will see an illustration of the thyroid’s access. I refer this Endocrine relationship as “**The Hypothalamic – Pituitary – Thyroid Axis**”. You may have heard many relationships between other three organs such as the HPA axis, but this one is no less important. Every relationship or communication axis between the hypothalamus, pituitary, and any endocrine gland has the utmost importance to our health. When there is a hypothalamic miscommunication, regardless of the dynamic between these bodies, there will be a dysfunction of the endocrine system.

On the right hand side of our image you will see the hypothalamus. Remember that this organ produces the ever-dynamic proopiomelanocortin (**POMC**) which becomes the thyrotropin releasing hormone which tells the pituitary to release TSH in turn. You may have heard of TSH or **thyroid stimulating hormone**. TSH then stimulates the thyroid, via an enzyme called **thyroid peroxidase** or TPO, to put iodine molecules on a big molecule called thyroglobulin. Thyroglobulin becomes T4. T4 takes its name from the four iodine molecules placed upon it by the thyroid, likewise T3 has three iodine molecules placed upon it.

There are two types of T3, the **active T3** and then the hormone called **reverse T3**. Reverse T3 is made in the minority, unless the wrong iodine molecule is pulled off thyroglobulin, mostly likely occurring within peripheral tissues or more rarely, in the thyroid. Should this occur, the main supply of T3 will not be active, resulting in blood tests finding that the patient has normal levels of T4, T3, and TSH. But this result would be deceptive as the patient is suffering from inactive thyroid hormone function, which is making the reverse hormone. The prevalence of patients with both hypothyroid symptoms and false positive blood tests necessitates the detail to which we examine the Thyroid in this text.

High cortisol levels will increase the liver’s glycogen stores, T3 needs sugar to increase mitochondria energy production. Therefore, the liver and adrenals must be healthy in order for your thyroid function to be healthy.

So why is the Thyroid so very important to our development? The fact is, the thyroid has a major effect on **fetal brain development**. Thyroid function affected our brain development when we were in the womb. If maternal thyroid production is not normal then the baby’s brain development will be threatened. Our children are dependent on their parent’s thyroid production increasing in pregnancy. If a pregnant mother has low T3 production, perhaps from hypothyroidism or autoimmune thyroiditis, her child’s brain development is in danger due to her low thyroid levels. She will not be producing enough thyroid hormone in order to facilitate normal fetal development. This is especially critical in the first eight weeks of development because that is when the baby is **dependent on the mother’s hormone production**. So, it is very important that if a person does not have a healthy thyroid they must get their thyroid healthy before becoming pregnant. If the baby does not have enough thyroid hormone exposure in early development, the brain function of that child will be affected and learning disabilities may be the result.

sections.title: Thyroid Dysfunction
sections.text:
The image on the left details the signs of thyroid dysfunction, with **hypothyroidism** on the left and hyperthyroidism on the right. “Hypo” meaning too low, while “Hyper” meaning too high, opposite terms to one another. When a person is **hypothyroid**, they have really low energy. We have talked about the experience of energy in relation to the adrenals, remember that low energy is marked by feeling low all day long followed by a crash in the afternoon. The low energy experience caused by the thyroid is a little different. The patient will also be tired but if they keep active they may find that they actually feel better. Activity will stimulate some thyroid induced energy, but as soon as the patient sits still, they crash and may fall asleep. Typical of low thyroid function, as opposed to the experience caused by hyperthyroidism, the patient feels “revved up” to the point of exhaustion. Almost as if their internal engine is firing on all cylinders all the time. Furthermore, Hypothyroid patients are typically depressed. They tend to experience foggy thinking as there is not enough T3 function to get those nerve transmitters going. Their hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows will thin, especially notably on the outer third of the eyebrow. Such patients often become constipated. As their metabolism slows they tend to gain weight.

> **[Graphic]** Slide "Signs of thyroid dysfunction." Hypothyroid: low energy (falls asleep if sitting still), depressed mood, foggy thinking, thin hair/lashes/brows, constipation, weight gain. Hyperthyroid: revved up to exhaustion, weight loss, bone loss, heart palpitations, diarrhea, anxiety.

**Hyperthyroid** is just the opposite, in the sense that because the system is flush with so much thyroid hormone, the metabolism begins burning the body as fuel. Such patients will lose weight and bone to this ravenous hunger. When those T4 levels are too high then patients will experience their heart racing as well as palpitations. Their bowels are racing to match the cardiovascular and metabolism. The patient may get diarrhea, matching feelings of anxiety rather than the depression of hypothyroidism. Typical of Graves’ disease are the bulging eyes. The muscles and fat behind the eye swell, pushing the eye forward, and so the eye starts to bulge. This bulging is a noteworthy condition that allows medical professionals to catch hyperthyroidism early. The eye structure changes are not normal.

> **[Graphic]** Illustrated chart "Thyroid dysfunction." Hypothyroidism: dry coarse hair, loss of eyebrow hair, puffy face, enlarged thyroid (goiter), slow heartbeat, arthritis, cold intolerance, depression, dry skin, fatigue, forgetfulness, heavy periods, infertility, muscle aches, weight gain, constipation, brittle nails. Hyperthyroidism: hair loss, bulging eyes, sweating, goiter, rapid heartbeat, difficulty sleeping, heat intolerance, infertility, irritability, muscle weakness, nervousness, scant periods, weight loss, frequent bowel movements, warm moist palms, finger tremor, soft nails.

Refer to the image on the right for reference on the effects of either condition on the body. Suffers of either condition will eventually be exhausted because their thyroid hormones are off which is a markedly different type of fatigue. In the image we see a woman with all these thyroid issues, split by sides between hypothyroid and hyperthyroidism. You will also find that even in hyperthyroidism there is hair loss as the body revs up the metabolism, which canabalizes any tissue.

Both hyper and hypothyroid patients have a tendency towards developing goiters, an exponential thyroid growth that causes a noticeable mass to develop in the neck. Both such patients will have trouble sleeping, although hyperthyroid patients sleep hot while hypothyroid patients sleep cold. Hyperthyroid patients and hypothyroid patients also share a mutual risk of infertility issues, as the normal menstrual cycle is disrupted by thyroid dysfunction. In hyperthyroid patients we can observe tremors from their system’s tension and they tend to be warm and moist versus cold. Hypothyroid patients may not be generally cold but they will definitely have cold hands and feet.

sections.title: The Basal Body Temperature Test
sections.text:
> **[Graphic]** Slide "Basal body temperature (BBT) test": take an oral temperature first thing in the morning; normal is 97.8–98.2°F; compare readings at the same point in the menstrual cycle (temperature rises naturally at ovulation); armpit (axillary) temperature is inaccurate in middle-aged people.

Okay, so basal body temperature test measures T3 activity. It gives medical image professionals (and can give you) an idea of what is happening to your thyroid functions at the tissue level. Remember T3 has to get into your cells in order to increase mitochondrial energy production, and increased energy production means an increased body temperature. What you do is you take your body temperature first thing in the morning. Now, I prefer a thermometer that gives **oral body temperature**, as opposed to an under the arm body temperature test. The reason for that is that most of my patients are in their midlife and they are having some issues with their skin being hotter than their core. They could be having hot flashes and have a very cold core temperature. The normal oral body temperature taken first thing in the morning is 97.8 to 98.2 Fahrenheit. This test can be measured monthly.

If you are still menstruating, take your basal temperature on the same days of your cycle each month — ideally days 2 through 4 of your period — because temperature rises after ovulation. Be sure to consider the day you will plan to take your tests, as **dependability is essential**. If you are no longer menstruating, test on the same calendar day each month — for example, always on the tenth. I usually advise taking it two or three mornings in a row and averaging the readings. Again, taking your temperature under your arm is not the best sample of temperature regulation, so I recommend sticking with oral. A good digital oral thermometer works well; while mercury thermometers are more accurate, they are no longer recommended because of the risk of mercury exposure if they break. What matters most is **using the same thermometer** each time.
